title: FanoutCache.transact()
text:
A write transaction on the shard key lives in, for with cache.transact(key='total') as tx:.


Usage
Source


FanoutCache.transact(*, key, retry=False)


It is Cache.transact() on that one shard: tx is this FanoutCache, calls on this thread inside the block for keys on that shard run in the transaction (through any handle on the root), it commits when the block exits and rolls back if the block raises, and a nested transact for a key on the same shard joins it. Other threads’ and processes’ writes to that shard wait for it; the other shards are not locked.
Inside the block, a call on this thread for a key on any other shard raises ValueError, reads included, through any handle on the root, and so does a transact for a key on another shard (its writes could not be in the transaction). Use shard_of to check that keys share a shard. Calls over every shard raise ValueError on this thread inside the block too: len(), volume(), iter(), iterkeys() (and next() on an iterator made before the block), clear(), expire(), cull() and checkpoint(). They would run inside the transaction on its shard and outside it on the others.
The check costs one atomic load while no transaction is open anywhere in the process; while one is (any thread’s, any cache’s), keyed calls, calls over every shard and iterator next()s also look at each shard that holds one.
As on Cache, a transaction belongs to a thread, not an asyncio task, a block that didn’t commit raises TransactionAborted at its exit, and under durable=True a failure to begin, or inside the block, raises.


Parameters


key: Key

Keyword-only. Any key on the shard to hold; it needn’t exist.

retry: bool = False

As for Cache.transact().

retry: bool = False

On a Timeout, try again until the call gets through, each round with the whole timeout, a durable=True handle included. Only Timeout is retried.





Raises


 TypeError

key isn’t a str, or retry isn’t a bool.





Examples
with cache.transact(key='totals:2026-11') as tx:
    n = tx.get('totals:2026-11', 0)
    tx.set('totals:2026-11', n + 1)

title: FanoutCache
text:
A disk cache split over several SQLite databases (shards), so reads and writes on different keys


Usage
Source


FanoutCache(
    directory,
    timeout=None,
    *,
    shards=None,
    size_limit=None,
    cull_limit=None,
    eviction_policy=None,
    serializer="msgpack",
    pickle=False,
    types=None,
    clock=None,
    max_connections=None,
    sqlite_cache_size=None,
    wal_size_limit=None,
    wal_checkpoint="manual",
    on_decode_error=None,
    durable=False
)


don’t queue on one file’s locks.
Each key lives in exactly one shard, chosen by a hash that is part of the on-disk format: every process, and every release, sends a key to the same shard. The root records its shard count, so every handle agrees on it. Single-key calls behave exactly as on Cache, on the key’s shard. len() and volume() add up every shard under one timeout.
clear(), expire(), cull() and checkpoint() run on every shard in turn, under one timeout for the whole call. If a shard fails, the others are still done, and then the first failure raises, as its own type (so except Timeout still works), with two extra attributes and a note naming them:

failed_shards: a tuple of the indexes of the shards that failed, in order.
removed (not on checkpoint()): how many entries the call removed in all, from every shard, including what a failed shard removed before it failed.



Parameters


directory: str | os.PathLike[str]

The root directory. It holds the manifest (diskcache-oxide-fanout) and one directory per shard, 000 to NNN. It must not be a plain Cache’s directory.

timeout: float | None = None

As for Cache (default 60). Opening, len(), volume(), clear(), expire(), cull(), checkpoint() and close() share one timeout across every shard, not one each.

shards: int | None = None

How many shards, 1 to 256. None (the default) uses the count the root records, or 8 for a new root. A count that differs from the recorded one raises LayoutMismatchError (a ValueError): changing it needs a new directory. Each shard takes about 4 file descriptors to open, and 2 more per connection it opens in use, so 256 shards need over 1,024: more than Linux’s default ulimit -n. Too few raises OSError (EMFILE) with the numbers.

size_limit: int | None = None

The disk budget in bytes for the whole cache, split evenly (floored) across the shards, each of which culls on its own. Each shard needs at least 1 MiB, so the total must be at least shards MiB. With none given, a new root gets 1 GiB in all.

cull_limit: int | None = None

As for Cache, per shard.

eviction_policy: Literal["least-recently-stored", "none"] | None = None

As for Cache, on every shard.

serializer: str = "msgpack"

As for Cache.

pickle: bool = False

As for Cache.

clock: Callable[[], float] | None = None

As for Cache.

max_connections: int | None = None

The most SQLite connections this process opens for the whole cache, split across the shards (the first max_connections % shards get one more). At least shards. The default is two per shard, and never fewer than 8 in all.

sqlite_cache_size: int | None = None

As for Cache, per connection.

wal_size_limit: int | None = None

As for Cache, per shard (each shard has its own write-ahead log).

wal_checkpoint: Literal["manual", "auto"] = "manual"

As for Cache.

on_decode_error: Literal["raise", "miss"] | Callable[[str, Exception], object] | None = None

As for Cache.

durable: bool = False

As for Cache: single-key calls on a shard that fails give their miss values. One report covers every shard, named by the root directory.





Raises


 ValueError

A setting is out of range, or max_connections is below shards.

 LayoutMismatchError

shards differs from the root’s, or the directory belongs to a plain Cache (or a shard of it does). Also a ValueError, and a FormatMismatchError.

 TypeError

An argument has the wrong type, including a bool for timeout or shards.

 FormatMismatchError

The root’s manifest, or a shard’s database, is in a format this version can’t read.

 OSError

The filesystem doesn’t support hard links, which creating the manifest needs, or the process can’t open enough files for every shard (ulimit -n).

 Timeout

A shard stayed locked, or a fork stayed pending, for longer than timeout.





Examples
from diskcache_oxide import FanoutCache

cache = FanoutCache('/var/cache/my-app-counters', shards=8)   # shards is keyword-only
cache.incr('ip:203.0.113.7')          # as on Cache, on the key's shard
cache.shard_of('ip:203.0.113.7')      # 0 to 7, the same in every process and release
with cache.transact(key='totals') as tx:   # one shard's write lock, not all of them
    tx.set('totals', tx.get('totals', 0) + 1)

title: Cache
text:
A disk cache backed by SQLite, shared safely across threads and processes.


Usage
Source


Cache(
    directory,
    timeout=None,
    *,
    size_limit=None,
    cull_limit=None,
    eviction_policy=None,
    serializer="msgpack",
    pickle=False,
    types=None,
    clock=None,
    max_connections=None,
    sqlite_cache_size=None,
    wal_size_limit=None,
    wal_checkpoint="manual",
    on_decode_error=None,
    durable=False
)


Every thread and process that opens the same directory shares one cache. The API follows diskcache.Cache; the deliberate differences are listed in the Divergences guide.


Parameters


directory: str | os.PathLike[str]

The cache directory. It’s created (owner-only, 0700) if it doesn’t exist.

timeout: float | None = None

Seconds a call waits for a lock or a pending fork before raising Timeout (default 60). It has to exceed work in flight plus a fork: see the Concurrency and Forks guide.

size_limit: int | None = None

The disk budget in bytes, database plus value files (default 1 GiB, minimum 1 MiB). Stored in the cache, so it applies to every process.

cull_limit: int | None = None

How many least-recently-stored entries a set() evicts when the cache is over size_limit (default 10).

eviction_policy: Literal["least-recently-stored", "none"] | None = None

'least-recently-stored' (a new cache’s default) evicts the oldest stored entries when over size_limit; 'none' never evicts for size, only removing expired entries, so the cache can grow past size_limit. Stored in the cache, so it applies to every process, and every write reads it afresh. None keeps the stored one. 'least-recently-used' and 'least-frequently-used' raise ValueError (D-022).

serializer: str = "msgpack"

'msgpack' (the default) or 'json', for values that aren’t plain str or bytes.

pickle: bool = False

Allow pickle for values the serializer can’t represent exactly. Without it, such values raise TypeError and pickled values are never read. Once the encoder has used a registration (types, or the global registry) for any part of a value, that value is never pickled: it is stored through the registration, or raises.

types: TypeRegistry | None = None

A TypeRegistry consulted before the process-wide diskcache_oxide.registry, for a cache that needs its own encoding of a type. Register types at import time, in every process that opens the directory, since a row written through a registration can only be read where it is registered.

clock: Callable[[], float] | None = None

A function returning the current time in seconds, used instead of the native clock. Tests pass clock=lambda: time.time() to follow a patched time.time.

max_connections: int | None = None

The most SQLite connections this process opens for the directory, shared by every handle on it (default 8).

sqlite_cache_size: int | None = None

SQLite’s page cache per connection, in 4 KiB pages (default 256, 1 MiB).

wal_size_limit: int | None = None

The write-ahead log is trimmed back to half this many bytes whenever it resets (default 64 MiB, minimum 1 MiB).

wal_checkpoint: Literal["manual", "auto"] = "manual"

'manual' (the default) leaves checkpoints to checkpoint() and close(). 'auto' also checkpoints after writes once the log is over wal_size_limit.

on_decode_error: Literal["raise", "miss"] | Callable[[str, Exception], object] | None = None

What a read does with a stored value it can’t decode. 'raise' (the default, unless durable=True, where it’s 'miss') raises. 'miss' treats it as a miss, logs a warning on the diskcache_oxide logger, and deletes the row if no build could ever read it (a class removed since it was pickled, malformed bytes). A row another version or host might read (ForeignValueError) is left in place. A callable does the same as 'miss', but is called with (key, exc) instead of the warning, after the row is dealt with; whatever it raises is logged. UnsafeValueError, Timeout, MemoryError and other errors that aren’t about the stored bytes raise, though under durable=True a Timeout, OSError or RecursionError from a pickle hook is a miss, with the row kept, and so is a RecursionError from a value too deep for this thread’s stack. Covers get, cache[key] and pop, which decodes before it deletes, so it keeps a row it can’t read. Under 'raise', pop still deletes a value no build could read, then raises.

durable: bool = False

Keep the cache from taking a request down, for an app whose every caller can fall back to its source of truth (default False). An outage on a single-key call (a Timeout, a full disk, an I/O error, a damaged database) doesn’t raise: get, pop and in give the default or False, set, add, touch and delete give False, and incr and decr give default + delta. It’s reported on the diskcache_oxide logger, at most once a minute per kind of failure. Bugs still raise (TypeError, ValueError, UnsafeValueError), as do MemoryError and KeyboardInterrupt, a RecursionError from encoding a value too deep for this thread’s stack, the constructor, admin calls (len, volume, clear, expire, cull, checkpoint, iteration) and anything inside a transaction held on this cache. This isn’t durability in the database sense: this option can drop writes, and a dropped set, delete, pop or incr means stale data until the entry expires, or forever if it has no expiry. See “A cache that can’t take a request down” in the Getting Started guide before you use it.





Raises


 ValueError

A setting is out of range, such as a size_limit under 1 MiB.

 TypeError

An argument has the wrong type, including a bool for timeout.

 FormatMismatchError

The directory holds a database in a format this version can’t read.

 LayoutMismatchError

The directory is a FanoutCache root or one of its shards. Also a ValueError, and a FormatMismatchError.

 Timeout

Another process held the database locked, or a fork stayed pending, for longer than timeout.





Examples
from diskcache_oxide import Cache

cache = Cache('/var/cache/my-app', timeout=1.0)  # every worker opens the same directory

cache.set('user:42', {'name': 'Sam', 'roles': {'admin'}}, expire=300)
cache.get('user:42')             # the dict, with roles still a set; None on a miss
cache['greeting'] = 'hello'      # never expires
if cache.add('job:nightly', 1, expire=3600):  # exactly one process wins
    run_nightly_job()
cache.close()                    # or `with Cache(...) as cache:`

title: Single-use keys
text: At 2 a.m. a tired user double-clicks a password reset link, and two requests arrive on two workers a few milliseconds apart. Both find the token. Both accept it. Some things must happen exactly once however many times they’re asked for: a reset link is good for one click, a verification code for one entry, a payment request for one charge even when the client retries. Two cache calls are atomic across every worker on the machine, pop() and add(), and between them they cover all of these.

title: Single-use keys
section: Short codes need an attempt limit
text:
Short codes need an attempt limit
A six-digit verification code is guessable, so pair it with a counter, created with an expiry the way the rate limiting recipe does, and burn the code after a few wrong guesses:
def check_code(user_id: int, entered: str) -> bool:
    attempts_key = f'verify-attempts:{user_id}'
    code_key = f'verify-code:{user_id}'
    tokens.add(attempts_key, 0, expire=10 * 60)
    if tokens.incr(attempts_key) > 5:
        tokens.delete(code_key)                   # too many tries: the code is dead
        return False
    if tokens.get(code_key) != entered:
        return False
    return tokens.pop(code_key) == entered        # right, and good for one entry only
The last line uses pop() so that two requests entering the right code at the same moment can’t both pass: only one of them gets the code back.

title: Using the cache from asyncio
text: An async framework makes one promise to every request it’s serving: nothing blocks the loop. A synchronous cache call looks like a small risk to that promise, and whether it is depends entirely on which call. diskcache-oxide’s API is synchronous. An AsyncCache is planned as an experiment, to ship only if it earns its place (see the roadmap), but the sync cache already works well in an asyncio app, provided you know which calls can block the event loop and for how long. Here are the three rules.

title: Using the cache from asyncio
text:
Fire and forget
When the response shouldn’t wait for the write at all, schedule it as a task. Keep a reference to the task until it finishes, or the loop may drop it half done:
background: set[asyncio.Task] = set()

def cache_later(key: str, value: object, expire: float) -> None:
    task = asyncio.create_task(asyncio.to_thread(cache.set, key, value, expire=expire))
    background.add(task)
    task.add_done_callback(background.discard)

title: Work queues
text:
A web request needs a thumbnail rendered, an email sent or a transcript cleaned up, and none of it should make the user wait. The usual answer is a queue and a worker, and the usual queue is Redis. On one machine a cache directory does the job: push() adds an item at one end, pull() takes one from the other, and every process that opens the directory shares the queue.

import tempfile

from diskcache_oxide import Cache

jobs = Cache(tempfile.mkdtemp(), eviction_policy='none')

for episode in (510, 511, 512):
    jobs.push({'episode': episode, 'step': 'transcode'}, prefix='transcode')

key, job = jobs.pull(prefix='transcode')
print(key, job)

transcode-500000000000000 {'episode': 510, 'step': 'transcode'}



How it works

A queue is a range of keys. push(value, prefix='transcode') stores the item under 'transcode-500000000000000', then ...001, and so on; with no prefix the keys are ints. side='front' pushes to the other end, and pull(side='back') takes the newest item, so the same calls make a stack or a deque.
Each item goes to exactly one worker. pull() reads the front item, then deletes exactly the version it read; a worker that loses that race to another reads the new front, and since every lost race is another worker’s progress, the queue always drains. Run as many workers, in as many processes, as you like.
Nothing is lost to a reader that can’t read it. An item this process can’t decode stays at the front for a worker that can. A pickled item on a pickle=False cache raises UnsafeValueError. A value of a type only a newer deploy has registered raises too, or with on_decode_error='miss', pull() returns the default. Either way this worker can take nothing behind that item until a worker that can read it pulls it. An item no build could read (damaged bytes) is removed: by default pull() then raises CorruptValueError, and with on_decode_error='miss' it logs the item and moves on to the next one.
peek() looks without taking. It takes no lock in the normal case, so any number of processes can watch a queue at once. peekitem() gives the newest or oldest entry of the whole cache, queue or not.


print(jobs.peek(prefix='transcode'))                # the next item, left in place
print(jobs.peek(prefix='transcode', side='back'))   # the newest
print(len(jobs))                                    # every entry in the cache

('transcode-500000000000001', {'episode': 511, 'step': 'transcode'})
('transcode-500000000000002', {'episode': 512, 'step': 'transcode'})
2




A worker loop
pull() returns (None, None) when the queue is empty, or the default you pass.

import time

def work(job: dict) -> None:
    print('transcoding', job['episode'])

def drain(cache: Cache, idle_sleep: float = 0.5, stop_after_idle: int = 1) -> None:
    idle = 0
    while idle < stop_after_idle:
        key, job = cache.pull(prefix='transcode')
        if key is None:
            idle += 1
            time.sleep(idle_sleep)
            continue
        idle = 0
        work(job)

drain(jobs, idle_sleep=0.01)

transcoding 511
transcoding 512


A real worker runs with no idle limit and sleeps between empty pulls; there’s no blocking pull to wait on.


Jobs that must survive a crash
A pulled item is gone as soon as pull() returns, so a worker that crashes halfway through work() loses it. If a job must survive that, give each job an id of its own and move it to a running record in the same transaction as the pull, so no crash can fall between the two. Delete the record when the work is done, and have a sweeper push back any record older than its lease:

import uuid

def enqueue(cache: Cache, episode: int) -> None:
    cache.push({'id': uuid.uuid4().hex, 'episode': episode, 'step': 'transcode'}, prefix='transcode')

def take(cache: Cache) -> dict | None:
    """The next job, recorded as running in the same transaction; None if the queue is empty."""
    with cache.transact():
        key, job = cache.pull(prefix='transcode')
        if key is None:
            return None
        cache.set(f"running:{job['id']}", (time.time(), job))   # no expire: the sweeper decides
    return job

def finish(cache: Cache, job: dict) -> None:
    cache.delete(f"running:{job['id']}")

def requeue_stale(cache: Cache, lease: float = 600) -> int:
    requeued = 0
    for record in cache.iterkeys(prefix='running:'):   # deleting while iterating is safe
        with cache.transact():
            started, job = cache.get(record, (None, None))   # read again: the worker may have finished
            if started is not None and time.time() - started > lease:
                cache.push(job, prefix='transcode', side='front')
                cache.delete(record)
                requeued += 1
    return requeued

enqueue(jobs, 513)
if (job := take(jobs)) is not None:
    work(job)
    finish(jobs, job)

enqueue(jobs, 514)
job = take(jobs)                          # this worker dies before it calls finish()
print(requeue_stale(jobs, lease=0), 'requeued:', jobs.peek(prefix='transcode'))

if (job := take(jobs)) is not None:       # another worker picks it up
    work(job)
    finish(jobs, job)

transcoding 513
1 requeued: ('transcode-500000000000000', {'id': 'a43a9d91c77b4252a73ec3d81b4c446b', 'episode': 514, 'step': 'transcode'})
transcoding 514


The sweeper reads each record again inside its transaction, so a job that finished while the sweeper was looking isn’t pushed back. One that is still running past its lease is, and then runs twice: make the lease longer than your slowest job, and make the work safe to repeat. Run the sweeper from one place, a scheduled job that one worker claims. The item’s key isn’t a lasting id (see below), which is why the job carries its own.


Several queues, and priorities
Each prefix is its own queue, in the same directory. A worker that serves more than one, or serves urgent work first, tries them in order:

jobs.push({'to': 'sam@example.com', 'template': 'welcome'}, prefix='email')
jobs.push({'episode': 515, 'step': 'transcode'}, prefix='transcode')
jobs.push({'episode': 516, 'step': 'transcode'}, prefix='urgent')

def next_job(cache: Cache, queues: tuple[str, ...] = ('urgent', 'transcode', 'email')) -> tuple[str, dict] | None:
    for queue in queues:
        key, job = cache.pull(prefix=queue)
        if key is not None:
            return queue, job
    return None

while (taken := next_job(jobs)) is not None:
    print(taken)

('urgent', {'episode': 516, 'step': 'transcode'})
('transcode', {'episode': 515, 'step': 'transcode'})
('email', {'to': 'sam@example.com', 'template': 'welcome'})


While the urgent queue keeps filling, the others wait. To count what’s waiting, iterate the queue’s keys: iterkeys(prefix='transcode-') is an indexed range scan over that queue alone. Items that expired but haven’t been removed yet are counted too, as are any other keys that start with 'transcode-'.


Cancelling and expiring jobs
A job pushed with tag= can be cancelled with the rest of its group, wherever they are in the queue, by evict(tag). A job that’s pointless after a deadline, a “your export is ready” email, say, can be pushed with expire=, and pull() passes over it once it has expired.

for episode in (520, 521):
    jobs.push({'episode': episode, 'step': 'transcode'}, prefix='transcode', tag='upload:batch-7')
jobs.push({'episode': 522, 'step': 'transcode'}, prefix='transcode')

print(jobs.evict('upload:batch-7'), 'cancelled; next:', jobs.pull(prefix='transcode'))

2 cancelled; next: ('transcode-500000000000002', {'episode': 522, 'step': 'transcode'})


pull(tag=True) and pull(expire_time=True) return the item’s tag and expiry beside it, as get() does: ((key, value), expire_time, tag).


In an app that uses FanoutCache
The queue calls are on Cache only: a queue spread over shards would have no order. If your app’s main cache is a FanoutCache, open the queue as a plain Cache in a directory of its own. A Cache opened on the FanoutCache’s directory raises LayoutMismatchError.
cache = FanoutCache('/var/cache/my-app', shards=8)
jobs = Cache('/var/cache/my-app-jobs', eviction_policy='none')
A separate directory is a good idea in any app: the queue gets its own eviction policy, and switching the main cache off can’t touch it.


Things to know

Open the queue’s cache with eviction_policy='none'. Least-recently-stored eviction removes the oldest entries first, and the oldest entry in a queue is the next one to be pulled: a full cache would silently drop the front of the queue. Under 'none' nothing is evicted for size; only items you gave an expire ever vanish.
Use a prefix no other key starts with. Only keys of exactly the queue’s shape ('{prefix}-' and 15 digits) belong to it, so an ordinary key like 'transcode-settings' or 'transcode-512', or an item of another queue named 'transcode-hd', is never pulled or numbered as one of its items (D-054). Keys whose next character after the dash is a digit, like 'transcode-512', do sort inside the queue’s range, though, and every queue call has to step past them.
Expired items are passed over. An item pushed with expire= is never pulled or peeked after it expires. It stays on disk, and keeps its number, until expire() or the cleanup that later writes do removes it.
Keys are reused. After the front item is pulled, a push to the front takes its number again, so don’t use an item’s key as a lasting id.
Inside a transaction, push() and pull() join it, and a rollback puts a pulled item back, after your code has already seen it.
Keep the queue out of NullCache’s reach. A NullCache has the queue calls, but its queue is always empty and its pushes store nothing, so a setting that switches caching off would drop every job. Don’t register the queue’s cache where it can be switched off.
durable=True can drop a push. On a durable handle a push() that fails returns None, and the job was never stored. Check the return value, or open the queue’s cache without durable.
Past the end, after 500 trillion pushes to one side, push() raises OverflowError rather than overwrite anything (D-057).

title: Caching responses from other services
text:
Your dashboard endpoint takes 1.2 seconds, and 1.1 of them are spent waiting for a partner API to return the same JSON it returned to the previous request. An app that calls other services (a payments API, a headless CMS, your own microservices) spends most of its latency waiting on them, and most of those answers don’t change between calls. Caching them in a directory every worker shares means one request to the upstream per machine instead of one per worker, and a last known good answer to serve when the upstream is slow, or down, or has started returning the wrong thing with a 500.

A cached fetch
The entry holds the response body, its ETag and a freshness deadline taken from the upstream’s Cache-Control: max-age, with a default when there isn’t one. A fresh entry is returned without a request. A stale one is revalidated with If-None-Match, so an unchanged resource costs a 304 with no body. And if the request fails while there’s a stale entry, the stale entry is the answer.

import json
import re
import tempfile
from urllib.parse import urlsplit

import httpx

from diskcache_oxide import Cache

now = [1_000_000.0]                                   # a fake clock; in a real app use time.time()
cache = Cache(tempfile.mkdtemp(), clock=lambda: now[0])

def max_age(response: httpx.Response) -> float | None:
    m = re.search(r'max-age=(\d+)', response.headers.get('cache-control', ''))
    return float(m.group(1)) if m else None

def fetch_json(client: httpx.Client, url: str, *, default_ttl: float = 300, keep: float = 24 * 3600) -> object:
    key = ('http', 'GET', url)
    host = urlsplit(url).netloc                       # the tag, to drop one service's responses at once
    entry = cache.get(key)
    if entry is not None and now[0] < entry['fresh_until']:
        return json.loads(entry['body'])              # fresh: no request at all

    headers = {'If-None-Match': entry['etag']} if entry and entry['etag'] else {}
    try:
        response = client.get(url, headers=headers)
        if response.status_code != 304:
            response.raise_for_status()
    except httpx.HTTPError:
        if entry is not None:
            return json.loads(entry['body'])          # upstream trouble: the last good answer
        raise

    if response.status_code == 304:                   # unchanged: keep the body, extend its freshness
        entry['fresh_until'] = now[0] + (max_age(response) or default_ttl)
    else:
        entry = {
            'body': response.content,
            'etag': response.headers.get('etag'),
            'fresh_until': now[0] + (max_age(response) or default_ttl),
        }
    cache.set(key, entry, expire=keep, tag=host)
    return json.loads(entry['body'])

Here it runs against a mock upstream that counts its requests:

seen: list[str | None] = []

def upstream(request: httpx.Request) -> httpx.Response:
    seen.append(request.headers.get('If-None-Match'))
    headers = {'ETag': '"v1"', 'Cache-Control': 'max-age=60'}
    if request.headers.get('If-None-Match') == '"v1"':
        return httpx.Response(304, headers=headers)
    return httpx.Response(200, json={'episodes': [512, 513]}, headers=headers)

client = httpx.Client(transport=httpx.MockTransport(upstream))
url = 'https://api.example.com/episodes'

fetch_json(client, url)
fetch_json(client, url)                               # fresh: served from the cache
now[0] += 61
fetch_json(client, url)                               # stale: one conditional request, answered 304
print(f'{len(seen)} upstream requests; If-None-Match headers sent: {seen}')

2 upstream requests; If-None-Match headers sent: [None, '"v1"']


Why it’s shaped this way:

Freshness lives in the value, not in expire. The entry’s expire (keep) is how long a stale copy is worth holding on to for revalidation and outages. If freshness were the expiry, a stale entry would vanish just when it’s useful.
304 costs one small write. The body is kept and only fresh_until changes. A set() is needed because the deadline is inside the value; touch() only moves the entry’s expiry.
The key names the request. It’s a tuple of method and URL, so no string formatting is needed and a URL can’t run into the next field. If the response depends on who’s asking (an Authorization header, a tenant), add that identity to the tuple, ('http', 'GET', url, tenant_id), or one user’s data will be served to another.
Every set passes the tag. An overwrite without tag= leaves the entry untagged, so the 304 path tags its write too.



Dropping one service’s responses
Each entry is tagged with its upstream’s host, so when a service tells you its data changed (a CMS publish webhook, a deploy of your own microservice), evict drops everything cached from it in one call, whatever the URLs were:

fetch_json(client, 'https://api.example.com/episodes/512')
print(cache.evict('api.example.com'), 'responses removed')

2 responses removed


A tuple key has no string prefix, so iterkeys(prefix=...) can’t find these entries; the tag is how you reach them as a group. See Invalidating groups of keys.


Variations

Serving the bytes straight through. When your endpoint relays the upstream’s body, store response.content and the content-type, and return them as they are, without parsing. Bodies of 64 KiB or more are stored in their own file, so a large payload costs no more than a small one.
Negative caching. A 404 that costs a round trip every time is worth caching for a short while: store {'status': 404, 'fresh_until': ...} and return your own not-found from it. Don’t cache 5xx as answers; the stale-on-error path above already covers an upstream outage.
Headers not to keep. Drop Set-Cookie and anything else tied to the one connection before storing a response’s headers.
Only one worker should refetch. When many requests find the same stale entry at once, they all revalidate. 304s are cheap, so that’s usually fine. If the upstream charges per call, wrap the refetch in a claim as the stale-while-revalidate recipe does.

title: Server-side sessions
text:
Every request arrives with a cookie and a question: who is this? A session is the one piece of per-user state almost every web app keeps server side to answer it: who’s logged in, since when, with which roles. Keeping it in a cache directory means every worker sees the same session the instant it’s written, a login on one worker is a login on all of them, and there’s no database row per request and no Redis to run. The cookie holds only a random id.

Start, load, end

import secrets
import tempfile

from diskcache_oxide import Cache

now = [1_000_000.0]                                   # a fake clock; in a real app use time.time()
sessions = Cache(tempfile.mkdtemp(), clock=lambda: now[0], eviction_policy='none')

IDLE = 30 * 60          # a session ends after 30 minutes without a request
ABSOLUTE = 12 * 3600    # and 12 hours after login, however active

def start_session(user_id: int, roles: list[str]) -> str:
    sid = secrets.token_urlsafe(32)
    sessions.set(f'session:{sid}', {'user_id': user_id, 'roles': roles, 'started': now[0]}, expire=IDLE)
    sessions.set(f'user-sessions:{user_id}:{sid}', True, expire=ABSOLUTE)
    return sid

def load_session(sid: str) -> dict | None:
    data, expires_at = sessions.get(f'session:{sid}', expire_time=True)
    if data is None or now[0] - data['started'] > ABSOLUTE:
        return None
    if expires_at - now[0] < IDLE / 2:                # slide the idle timeout, but not on every request
        sessions.touch(f'session:{sid}', expire=IDLE)
    return data

def end_session(sid: str) -> None:
    data = sessions.pop(f'session:{sid}')
    if data is not None:
        sessions.delete(f'user-sessions:{data["user_id"]}:{sid}')

sid = start_session(42, ['member'])
now[0] += 20 * 60
print('after 20 min:', load_session(sid) is not None)   # active, and the timeout slides
now[0] += 20 * 60
print('after 40 min:', load_session(sid) is not None)   # still active: the last request was 20 min ago
now[0] += 31 * 60
print('after 71 min:', load_session(sid) is not None)   # idle too long

after 20 min: True
after 40 min: True
after 71 min: False



touch() slides the idle timeout without rewriting the session. It’s a small write, so it’s done only when less than half the idle time is left, which get(expire_time=True) tells you in the same read as the data. A busy user costs one write every 15 minutes instead of one per request.
The absolute lifetime is inside the value. expire can only say when the session dies if it’s left alone; the login time says when it dies regardless.
The id is the secret. secrets.token_urlsafe(32) in an HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookie, and nothing else in the cookie. The session dict holds ids and roles, not the whole user object, which belongs in the database.



Log out everywhere
A password change or a stolen laptop should end every session a user has. The second key written at login, user-sessions:{user_id}:{sid}, is an index for exactly this: a prefix scan finds them all.

other = start_session(42, ['member'])
sid = start_session(42, ['member'])

def end_all_sessions(user_id: int) -> int:
    ended = 0
    for key in sessions.iterkeys(prefix=f'user-sessions:{user_id}:'):
        sid = key.rsplit(':', 1)[1]
        ended += sessions.delete(f'session:{sid}')
        sessions.delete(key)
    return ended

print(end_all_sessions(42), 'sessions ended;', 'still valid:', load_session(other) is not None)

2 sessions ended; still valid: False


Index entries for sessions that idled out stay until their own ABSOLUTE expiry, which is why they have one. To show a user their active sessions, read each session: key the index names and skip the ones that are gone.


Sessions are not cache entries
A lost session is a forced logout, so sessions get a cache of their own, configured unlike the one for page fragments:

Nothing evicted for size. Eviction removes the least recently stored entries, and a long-lived session is exactly that. Open the session cache with eviction_policy='none', so a session goes only when it expires or ends. Sessions are small (a few hundred bytes each), so 1 GiB holds millions; watch volume() if you store more per session, since under 'none' the cache can grow past size_limit.
Never a NullCache. A NullCache stores nothing, so nobody could log in. If the app’s other caches can be switched off through Caches, register the session cache by name and leave it enabled.
Not durable=True. A dropped write there means a login that silently didn’t happen. Let set() raise and show the user an error.
Run expire() from a scheduled job, claimed by one worker, so ended sessions free their space. Expired sessions are already invisible to get(); this is housekeeping.
One machine. Every worker on the host shares the sessions. Behind a load balancer across several machines, use sticky sessions or a session store every machine can reach.

title: Testing code that uses a cache
text:
Code that uses a cache has a talent for passing its tests for the wrong reason: the second assertion was green because the first one left the answer behind, and the test that “covers” expiry sleeps for two seconds and hopes. Such code needs tests of two kinds: tests where caching shouldn’t get in the way, and tests of the caching behavior itself (is the value cached, does it expire, is it invalidated). diskcache-oxide gives you a tool for each, and neither involves sleeping.

A real cache per test
A Cache in pytest’s tmp_path is fast and isolated: each test gets its own empty cache, and it’s thrown away afterwards.
import pytest

from diskcache_oxide import Cache

@pytest.fixture
def cache(tmp_path):
    with Cache(tmp_path / 'cache') as cache:
        yield cache


No caching at all: NullCache
For tests that exercise your app rather than its caching, a cached value from an earlier test can hide a bug. Swap in a NullCache: every read misses and every write succeeds, so every call goes to the real code path. It has the same methods and signatures as Cache, so nothing else changes.
from diskcache_oxide import NullCache

@pytest.fixture
def app_cache(monkeypatch):
    null = NullCache()
    monkeypatch.setattr('my_app.services.cache', null)
    return null


Testing expiry without sleeping
diskcache-oxide reads the clock natively in Rust, so patching time.time doesn’t affect it on its own. Pass clock= instead. A small fake clock lets a test jump forward in time:

import tempfile

from diskcache_oxide import Cache

class FakeClock:
    def __init__(self, now: float = 1_000_000.0) -> None:
        self.now = now

    def __call__(self) -> float:
        return self.now

    def advance(self, seconds: float) -> None:
        self.now += seconds

clock = FakeClock()
cache = Cache(tempfile.mkdtemp(), clock=clock)

cache.set('session:abc', {'user': 42}, expire=30)
clock.advance(29)
print('after 29 s:', cache.get('session:abc'))
clock.advance(2)
print('after 31 s:', cache.get('session:abc'))

after 29 s: {'user': 42}
after 31 s: None


As a fixture:
@pytest.fixture
def clock():
    return FakeClock()

@pytest.fixture
def cache(tmp_path, clock):
    with Cache(tmp_path / 'cache', clock=clock) as cache:
        yield cache

def test_sessions_expire(cache, clock):
    cache.set('session:abc', {'user': 42}, expire=30)
    clock.advance(31)
    assert cache.get('session:abc') is None
If your tests already patch time.time (with unittest.mock, freezegun or time-machine) and you want the cache to follow along, pass clock=lambda: time.time(). The lambda looks up time.time on every call, so it sees the patched version.


Testing code that runs in several processes
Code that relies on the cache being shared, like a job claim or a rate limit, can be tested for real: start processes with multiprocessing and point them at the same tmp_path directory. diskcache-oxide is safe with every start method, including fork.
import multiprocessing

def claim(directory: str) -> bool:
    with Cache(directory) as cache:
        return cache.add('job:nightly', 'claimed', expire=60)

def test_only_one_worker_claims_the_job(tmp_path):
    with multiprocessing.Pool(8) as pool:
        results = pool.map(claim, [str(tmp_path)] * 8)
    assert results.count(True) == 1
A Cache also pickles: the copy a multiprocessing worker receives reopens the same directory with the same options, so you can pass the cache itself instead of its path.

title: Watching a cache in production
text:
A cache runs inside your workers for weeks without anyone looking at it, until a page gets slow or the disk fills up and someone asks whether the cache is working. Is it full? Is anything hitting it? Is the write-ahead log eating the disk? The numbers that answer those questions are cheap to read, so put them on a health endpoint or an admin page before you need them.

A health check
Everything here reads a few numbers and never waits on writers, so it’s fine to call on every health probe:

import os
import tempfile

from diskcache_oxide import Cache, CacheLike

cache = Cache(tempfile.mkdtemp(), size_limit=64 * 2**20)
cache.stats(enable=True)  # at startup, in every worker: counting is off until something turns it on

def wal_bytes(cache: CacheLike) -> int:
    if cache.directory is None:  # a NullCache
        return 0
    try:
        return os.path.getsize(os.path.join(cache.directory, 'diskcache-oxide.sqlite-wal'))
    except FileNotFoundError:
        return 0

def cache_health(cache: CacheLike) -> dict:
    hits, misses = cache.stats()
    lookups = hits + misses
    volume = cache.volume()
    return {
        'enabled': cache.enabled,
        'entries': len(cache),
        'volume_mib': round(volume / 2**20, 1),
        'percent_of_limit': round(100 * volume / cache.size_limit, 1),
        'eviction_policy': cache.eviction_policy,
        'hits': hits,
        'misses': misses,
        'hit_ratio': round(hits / lookups, 2) if lookups else None,
        'wal_mib': round(wal_bytes(cache) / 2**20, 1),
    }

for n in range(200):
    cache.set(f'page:{n}', 'x' * 20_000)
for n in range(300):
    cache.get(f'page:{n}')

print(cache_health(cache))

{'enabled': True, 'entries': 200, 'volume_mib': 3.9, 'percent_of_limit': 6.2, 'eviction_policy': 'least-recently-stored', 'hits': 200, 'misses': 100, 'hit_ratio': 0.67, 'wal_mib': 3.9}


Return it from an endpoint and you have something to graph or alert on. In Flask:
@app.get('/health/cache')
def health_cache() -> dict:
    return cache_health(cache)
In FastAPI the same function body works under @app.get('/health/cache'). Keep the endpoint behind your admin auth or on an internal port: the numbers aren’t secret, but there’s no reason to publish them.


What the numbers mean

enabled is False for a NullCache. If the cache comes from a Caches registry, that’s what a lookup hands out while the cache can’t open, so enabled: false on a cache you never switched off means something is wrong. The log says what.
len(cache) counts entries, including expired ones not yet removed. It’s read from a stored total, so it costs the same on a cache of ten entries or ten million.
volume() is the cache’s size in bytes: the database pages in use plus the value files. It leaves out the write-ahead log and pages freed by deletes, which SQLite keeps in the file for reuse, so du on the directory can show more. check(fix=True) (below) gives the freed pages back.
size_limit and eviction_policy. Under the default 'least-recently-stored', a full cache sits close to its limit, and that’s normal: each set() that finds it over the limit evicts the oldest entries. Under 'none' nothing is evicted for size, so percent_of_limit can pass 100. On a sessions or work queue cache, that’s the number to alert on. Both attributes are the values this process last saw; cache.reset('size_limit') and cache.reset('eviction_policy') read what’s stored now, in case another process changed them.
Hits and misses count get and cache[key] in this process. An expired entry, and a value answered as a miss by on_decode_error, count as misses. in, pop and iteration don’t count, and a durable=True outage answered as a miss counts as nothing. A FanoutCache sums its shards, and a NullCache always reports (0, 0).

A low hit ratio on a full 'least-recently-stored' cache can mean size_limit is too small for what you’re caching: entries are evicted before anyone reads them twice. Raise it with cache.reset('size_limit', 2 * 2**30), which every process picks up at its next write, or in the constructor for the next deploy.


Hits and misses across workers
The counts live in each process’s memory and are never written to the database, so reading them costs nothing. That also means a health probe that lands on one gunicorn worker sees that worker’s counts only, since its last restart; a forked child starts from zero. Every handle on one directory in a process shares one set of counts, and they survive closing the last handle.
For a total across workers, have each worker add its counts to a shared counter now and then, from a timer or after every few hundred requests. Keep those counters in a small cache of their own, so reading the totals doesn’t count as lookups in the cache you’re measuring:

counters = Cache(tempfile.mkdtemp())

def publish_stats(cache: Cache, counters: Cache) -> None:
    hits, misses = cache.stats(reset=True)
    counters.incr('pages:hits', hits)
    counters.incr('pages:misses', misses)

publish_stats(cache, counters)
cache.get('page:1')
publish_stats(cache, counters)
print('every worker:', counters.get('pages:hits'), 'hits,', counters.get('pages:misses'), 'misses')
print('this worker since:', cache.stats())

every worker: 201 hits, 100 misses
this worker since: (0, 0)


stats(reset=True) returns the counts and zeroes them in one call, so a lookup between the read and the reset isn’t lost. This is the counters recipe applied to the cache itself.


An admin page for every cache
A Caches registry gives you one row per cache with stats(). It opens each registered cache, and never raises: a cache that can’t be opened gets its error set, with the exception’s type and message.

import dataclasses

from diskcache_oxide import Caches

caches = Caches(tempfile.mkdtemp(), timeout=1.0)
caches.register('general')
caches.register('pages', size_limit=256 * 2**20)
caches['general'].set('greeting', 'hello')

for name, stat in caches.stats().items():
    print(dataclasses.asdict(stat) | {'directory': '...'})

{'name': 'general', 'directory': '...', 'enabled': True, 'count': 1, 'volume': 40960, 'error': None}
{'name': 'pages', 'directory': '...', 'enabled': True, 'count': 0, 'volume': 40960, 'error': None}


A cache that can’t open shows up here with count and volume at 0 and the reason in error, for example FormatMismatchError: cache format version 2 is not supported (this build uses version 3) ... after an upgrade that changed the format (see Upgrading across a format change).
As an endpoint, with each cache’s hit counts added. Every cache in this registry is a plain one; read a sharded one with caches.fanout(name) instead, since caches[name] raises TypeError for it:
@app.get('/admin/caches')
def admin_caches() -> dict:
    rows = {}
    for name, stat in caches.stats().items():
        hits, misses = caches[name].stats()
        rows[name] = dataclasses.asdict(stat) | {'hits': hits, 'misses': misses}
    return rows

@app.post('/admin/caches/<name>/clear')
def clear_cache(name: str) -> dict:
    return {'removed': caches.clear(name, timeout=10)}
caches.clear() raises if the cache can’t be opened, so the page never reports “0 removed” for a failure. It works on a disabled cache too. Give it a longer timeout= than the request path’s, since it holds the write lock once per chunk. For the rest of the registry’s admin calls, see Admin and shutdown.


The write-ahead log
wal_mib in the health check is the size of diskcache-oxide.sqlite-wal beside the database. At normal load wal_size_limit keeps it at a few MiB. A burst of writes with readers in other processes can leave it much larger, and in the default wal_checkpoint='manual' mode it stays that size until something checkpoints it.
If it keeps growing, call checkpoint() from a maintenance job. It returns True when the log was copied into the database and truncated, and False, without raising, when other processes kept it busy; try again later. If that isn’t enough, open the cache with wal_checkpoint='auto'. Storage and WAL has the details. A FanoutCache has one log per shard, in the shard folders (000/, 001/, …), so add those up for the total.


Checking for damage
check() compares the database with the value files and returns what it found as a list of warnings.WarningMessage, without issuing any warnings. An empty list means nothing is wrong. Here a value file is deleted behind the cache’s back:

import glob

damaged = Cache(tempfile.mkdtemp())
damaged.set('report', b'x' * 100_000)   # 64 KiB or more: stored in a file of its own
damaged.set('summary', 'small')
[path] = glob.glob(os.path.join(damaged.directory, '*', '*.val'))
os.remove(path)                          # what a bad disk or a stray rm would do

for warning in damaged.check():
    print(warning.category.__name__, str(warning.message).replace(damaged.directory, '...'))
print('repaired:', len(damaged.check(fix=True)), '| after:', damaged.check(), '| entries:', len(damaged))

UserWarning file not found: .../dd/dda96dcaae7cccde06efa2b3a473f2ed.val
repaired: 1 | after: [] | entries: 1


It reports SQLite’s integrity_check lines, value files that are missing or the wrong size, files nobody owns that are over an hour old, and stored totals that don’t match the rows. check(fix=True) also repairs: it removes entries whose files are missing or cut short (they read as misses anyway), removes unowned files in the value folders, corrects the totals, then runs VACUUM, which shrinks the database file to what’s in use, and checkpoints.
Run it from a scheduled job one worker claims, never from a health probe. integrity_check reads the whole database and VACUUM rewrites it, and writers and forks wait for both. VACUUM also needs room for a temporary copy of the database in SQLITE_TMPDIR, TMPDIR or /tmp.
import logging

log = logging.getLogger('my_app')

def nightly_cache_check() -> None:
    problems = cache.check()
    for warning in problems:
        log.warning('cache check: %s', warning.message)
    if problems:
        cache.check(fix=True)


Log lines to alert on
Where diskcache-oxide has been told not to raise, it logs on the diskcache_oxide logger instead, and that line is then the only sign anything happened. Make sure the logger reaches your log aggregator or Sentry:

A Caches cache that can’t open logs at ERROR with the traceback, once per retry, and hands out a NullCache meanwhile. An open that only timed out logs at WARNING.
durable=True logs swallowed failures at most once a minute per cache handle, with counts by operation: WARNING for a busy lock, ERROR for a full disk, an I/O error or a failed delete.
on_decode_error='miss' logs a warning for a stored value it couldn’t read.

The exact messages, and what to do about each, are in Errors and what to do about them.


Things to know

stats() turns counting on. Its enable argument defaults to True, so a health check that reads the counts also starts them. stats(enable=False) turns counting off and stops the counts where they are.
Counts reset on restart. Graph the hit ratio, not the raw counts, or publish the counts as above.
len() includes expired entries until expire(), or the cleanup a set() does, removes them. A scheduled expire() keeps it honest; caches.expire_all() does every registered cache.
Health checks shouldn’t write. Everything in cache_health is a read. check() and checkpoint() belong in a maintenance job.

title: Running a job once across workers
text:
At the top of the hour, eight gunicorn workers wake up at the same instant with the same idea: time for the hourly cleanup. Each one has its own copy of the scheduler, none of them knows the others exist, and the only thing they share is a cache directory. You want the job to run once, and it turns out the directory is enough.
add() stores a value only if the key is missing or expired, and it’s atomic across every thread and process using the cache directory. When several callers race to add the same key, exactly one gets True. That makes the key a claim on the job.

Claim the run
import os

from diskcache_oxide import Cache

cache = Cache('/var/cache/my-app')

def hourly_cleanup() -> None:
    if not cache.add('job:hourly-cleanup', os.getpid(), expire=55 * 60):
        return  # another worker has it this hour
    remove_stale_sessions()
The expire is the important part. It decides when the job can be claimed again, and it’s also what saves you if the worker that claimed the job crashes halfway through: the claim expires and the next run goes ahead. Set it a little shorter than the schedule’s interval, so the next run is never blocked by the previous claim.
Storing os.getpid() (or a hostname and pid) as the value costs nothing and makes it easy to see who claimed the job: cache.get('job:hourly-cleanup').


See it work
Here eight threads race for the same claim. Processes behave the same way.

import tempfile
import threading

from diskcache_oxide import Cache

cache = Cache(tempfile.mkdtemp())
winners = []
start = threading.Barrier(8)

def worker(n: int) -> None:
    start.wait()
    if cache.add('job:hourly-cleanup', n, expire=3300):
        winners.append(n)

threads = [threading.Thread(target=worker, args=(n,)) for n in range(8)]
for t in threads:
    t.start()
for t in threads:
    t.join()

print(f'{len(winners)} winner: worker {winners[0]}')
print('claim holds:', cache.get('job:hourly-cleanup'))

1 winner: worker 7
claim holds: 7




Jobs that should run once, then again as soon as they’re done
For work that isn’t on a fixed schedule (process the queue, rebuild the search index), use expire as a lease: a time limit after which a crashed worker’s claim lapses. Delete the key when the work finishes, so the next request can claim it right away.
def rebuild_search_index() -> None:
    if not cache.add('job:search-index', os.getpid(), expire=10 * 60):
        return
    try:
        do_rebuild()
    finally:
        cache.delete('job:search-index')
Make the lease comfortably longer than the job ever takes. If the job outlives it, a second worker can start a second copy.


Give claims their own small cache
Two things can make a claim vanish early, and both argue for keeping claims out of your main cache:

Switching caching off. A NullCache follows the rule “every entry expires the instant it’s written”, so its add() always returns True. With caching off, every worker’s claim succeeds and the job runs once per worker. That’s harmless for idempotent jobs and wrong for jobs with side effects, like sending email.
Eviction. When a cache is over its size_limit, it evicts the least recently stored entries, and a claim is exactly the kind of small, rarely written entry that goes first. If it’s evicted before it expires, a second worker can claim the job.

A separate cache directory just for coordination, which is never swapped for a NullCache and never evicts (eviction_policy='none', so only expired claims go), avoids both:
coordination = Cache('/var/cache/my-app-coordination', eviction_policy='none')
A claim is the right tool when a worker that loses should skip the job. When it should wait its turn instead, use a Lock or a BoundedSemaphore from Coordination, on the same coordination cache.

title: Divergences from python-diskcache
text:
diskcache-oxide’s test suite is a conformance suite: the same black-box tests run against real diskcache 5.6.3 and against diskcache-oxide. Where they behave differently, it’s on purpose, and it’s written down here. Running one suite against two implementations turned out to be a bug detector pointed in both directions: most of the differences below are diskcache bugs the suite found, each with a reproduction in the repository’s upstream/ folder.
A divergence is never a way to skip a failing test. The full record, including test names and measurements, is tests/DIVERGENCES.md.

title: Divergences from python-diskcache
text:
D-001: no pickle by default
diskcache pickles every value. diskcache-oxide stores str and bytes raw and everything else as msgpack or tagged JSON. A value the format can’t represent exactly raises TypeError at set() unless the cache was opened with pickle=True. A cache opened without it never unpickles: reading a pickled value written by a pickle=True peer raises UnsafeValueError and leaves the row alone. Unpickling runs code from whatever is in the cache directory, and silently pickling hides values that were never meant to be cached. See Serialization.

title: Divergences from python-diskcache
text:
D-015: owner-only directories
A cache directory diskcache-oxide creates, and its value-file subdirectories, are 0700. Existing directories are never changed. Anyone who can write to a cache directory can poison the cache, and its contents (keys with IP addresses in them, for example) can be private.

title: Divergences from python-diskcache
text:
D-021: directory is required
diskcache creates a temporary directory if you don’t give one. A cache directory is shared state and a security boundary, and an implicit temp directory is almost never what a multi-process app wants.

title: Divergences from python-diskcache
text:
D-008: NaN round-trips
In diskcache, set('k', float('nan')) succeeds but get('k') returns None, ignoring any default. In diskcache-oxide it’s a float like any other.

title: Divergences from python-diskcache
section: D-010: expire() removes everything that has expired
text:
D-010: expire() removes everything that has expired
diskcache’s expire() works in chunks of 100, and when expired entries share one expiry time it stops after the first chunk. With 250 such entries, one call removes 100. diskcache-oxide removes all of them, still in chunks so writers can get in between.

title: Divergences from python-diskcache
text:
D-011: clear() keeps concurrent writes
diskcache’s clear() keeps deleting until the cache is empty, including entries written while it runs. In a reproduction with 50,000 entries and a concurrent writer, it deleted 76,000 writes that had already succeeded, and its running time grew with the write rate. diskcache-oxide’s clear() removes only entries that existed when it started, and always finishes. evict(tag) is bounded the same way.

title: Divergences from python-diskcache
section: D-013 and D-016: large values under pressure
text:
D-013 and D-016: large values under pressure
If a large value’s file disappears, diskcache returns the default but the key still reads as present in in and len. diskcache-oxide treats it as a miss and removes the orphaned row.
When one process overwrites a large value while others read it, diskcache occasionally returns the default for a key that was never deleted, which makes callers recompute a hot value for nothing. diskcache-oxide’s readers detect the overwrite and retry, so they always get a whole value, old or new.

title: Divergences from python-diskcache
text:
D-014: no booleans for numbers
bool is an int subclass, so in diskcache expire=True is a one-second TTL and expire=False stores an already-expired entry. diskcache-oxide raises TypeError: a bool there is almost always an argument in the wrong position.

title: Divergences from python-diskcache
section: D-012: forks while another thread writes
text:
D-012: forks while another thread writes
When a process forks while another of its threads is in a write transaction, diskcache’s child inherits a lock nobody in the child will release, and its first write stalls for the full timeout (60 seconds by default). Under a busy read/write load that hits 20-50% of forks. diskcache-oxide’s fork barrier waits for in-flight transactions before the fork, so the child can always write. See Concurrency and forks.

title: Divergences from python-diskcache
section: D-020: forking inside your own transaction
text:
D-020: forking inside your own transaction
CPython won’t let a library stop a fork, and a transaction held by the forking thread itself can’t be waited for. In diskcache the child stalls behind it. In diskcache-oxide, the child’s copy of the transaction is poisoned and its writes to that database raise RuntimeError immediately, and the parent gets a RuntimeWarning.

title: Divergences from python-diskcache
section: D-029: tx is the cache, and every handle shares it
text:
D-029: tx is the cache, and every handle shares it
diskcache’s with cache.transact() as tx: binds tx to None, and a second Cache on the same directory has its own connection, so its transact() inside the first one’s block waits for the write lock until it times out. In diskcache-oxide tx is the cache itself, and on the thread that entered the block every call on that directory runs in the transaction, through any handle: a transact() on a second handle joins the outer one instead of waiting. Other threads’ calls never join it. See Transactions.

title: Divergences from python-diskcache
section: D-030: TransactionBusy, and what retry=True retries
text:
D-030: TransactionBusy, and what retry=True retries
Inside one cache’s transaction, diskcache’s transact() on a second cache waits for its write lock until it times out, and retry=True loops on any sqlite3.OperationalError. When another thread holds that lock, diskcache-oxide raises TransactionBusy, a Timeout subclass, at once: that thread could be waiting for a lock this one holds, and no timeout setting fixes that. retry=True retries a plain Timeout and never TransactionBusy, and checks for Ctrl-C between attempts.

title: Divergences from python-diskcache
section: D-031: a transaction can end on another thread
text:
D-031: a transaction can end on another thread
diskcache says a transaction “may not be shared between threads”. In diskcache-oxide any thread may commit or roll back the owner’s transaction through its __exit__, within the transaction’s timeout. A commit that can’t run in time raises Timeout and rolls back, and the owner’s own exit afterwards raises TransactionAborted (a RuntimeError) unless the transaction committed, so a with block never exits cleanly when its writes are gone. An owner’s exit during another thread’s commit waits for the outcome.

title: Divergences from python-diskcache
text:
D-017 and D-018: bounded connections
diskcache opens a connection for every thread that uses a cache, so 64 threads hold 131 files open in the cache directory, and close() closes only the calling thread’s connection. diskcache-oxide uses a pool per database file, at most max_connections (default 8), and the last close() closes every connection, so the directory is safe to move or delete afterwards.

title: Divergences from python-diskcache
text:
D-019: opening never writes
Opening an existing diskcache commits a write transaction even when nothing changed. diskcache-oxide’s open, and reads after it, never write, so a read-mostly worker or a read-only copy of the directory never takes the write lock.

title: Divergences from python-diskcache
text:
D-023: bounded SQLite memory
diskcache’s default is a 32 MiB page cache and a 64 MiB memory map per connection, with one connection per thread. diskcache-oxide’s sqlite_cache_size defaults to 256 pages (1 MiB) per pooled connection, so SQLite’s memory per directory stays around 8 MiB per process.

title: Divergences from python-diskcache
text:
D-024: a WAL that shrinks
With readers in other processes, a burst of writes makes SQLite’s write-ahead log grow to fit the burst and stay that size: hundreds of MiB to over 1 GiB beside a database of a few MiB. diskcache-oxide trims the log whenever it resets (wal_size_limit), offers checkpoint() to empty it on demand, checkpoints a large log at close(), and can checkpoint automatically with wal_checkpoint='auto', which tries a few times in a row so that a reader in flight in another process doesn’t defeat it. See Storage and WAL.

title: Divergences from python-diskcache
text:
FanoutCache (D-032 to D-040)
These are covered together in FanoutCache: sharded caches, and listed against diskcache’s in Switching from python-diskcache.

D-032: the shard count is part of where every key lives, so it’s recorded, and a different shards= is an error instead of a quiet loss of data and atomicity.
D-033: the hash is fixed by its definition and part of the format, and iterkeys(prefix=) gives FanoutCache the ordered listing Cache has.
D-034: a silently dropped write and a hang are both worse than an error the caller chose how to handle; durable=True is that choice.
D-035: a maintenance job must finish in bounded time, and when it can’t, it must say what it did.
D-036 and D-037: budgets (size, connections, file descriptors) follow configuration, not the number of threads or shards.
D-038: a typo shouldn’t leave a directory that neither kind of cache can open, or a shard written behind the FanoutCache’s back.
D-039: shards is keyword-only so that the second positional argument is timeout, as on Cache. The sub-collections and read() would each need their own design across shards, so they aren’t copied from diskcache (see the roadmap). Everything else on Cache, apart from the queue calls, works on a FanoutCache too.
D-040: holding every shard’s lock would serialize the whole cache behind one transaction, which is what sharding exists to avoid.

title: Coordination: locks, semaphores and throttles
text:
A cache directory is shared by every process on the machine that opens it, and add(), incr() and transact() are atomic across all of them. That makes it a place to coordinate work as well as cache it: one worker at a time on a job, at most a few at once on a slow API, a rate limit every worker respects. diskcache-oxide ships diskcache’s coordination recipes for that, under the same names.
from diskcache_oxide import Cache, Lock, RLock, BoundedSemaphore, Averager, throttle, barrier

locks = Cache('/var/cache/my-app/locks', eviction_policy='none')
Two common jobs don’t need a lock at all. When only one worker should run a job and the others should skip it, an add() claim is simpler: see Running a job once across workers. To hand work items to whichever worker is free, use a queue: see Work queues.

Lock
lock = Lock(locks, 'report:nightly', expire=600)

with lock:
    build_the_report()
One holder at a time, in any thread of any process. acquire() waits, polling every millisecond, until it gets the lock; release() gives it back; locked() says whether anyone holds it. It isn’t reentrant: the holder taking it again waits for itself. Give it an expire, so a holder that crashes without releasing doesn’t keep the lock forever.
RLock is the reentrant one: the thread holding it may take it again, and must release it as many times. Its owner is the process and thread, with a per-process nonce, so another thread, another process, a forked child, or a container on the same volume that happens to have the same pid can never release or re-enter it. Releasing a lock you don’t hold raises AssertionError.


BoundedSemaphore
api_slots = BoundedSemaphore(locks, 'api:partner', value=4)

with api_slots:
    call_the_partner_api()
At most value holders at once, everywhere. Releasing more times than it was acquired raises AssertionError.


throttle
@throttle(locks, count=10, seconds=1)
def send_webhook(event): ...
At most count calls every seconds, across every process: a token bucket stored under the function’s qualified name (or name=). A call with no token waits until one is due. Two fixes over diskcache’s: a bucket that expired or was cleared counts as full rather than raising TypeError, and decorating the function adds the bucket only if it isn’t there, so every worker that imports the module doesn’t refill it.


barrier
@barrier(locks, Lock)
def migrate(): ...
Runs the function under a lock made by the factory you pass (Lock, RLock, BoundedSemaphore, or your own), keyed by the function’s qualified name: one caller at a time.


Averager
latency = Averager(locks, 'latency:checkout')
latency.add(0.080)
latency.add(0.120)
latency.get()  # 0.1
A running average whose total and count are updated together in one transaction, so every process adding to it agrees.


memoize_stampede
memoize_stampede(cache, expire) is memoize with stampede protection: a result close to expiring is recomputed early, in a background thread, by one caller, while everyone else keeps getting the cached value. It’s a cache, not a lock, so it works on a NullCache and a durable=True cache as memoize does. See Caching expensive calls.


Things to know

Use a cache of its own for coordination, with eviction_policy='none'. Lock and semaphore keys are cache entries: least-recently-stored culling removes the oldest first, and a lock held a long time is old, so a full cache can evict a held lock. Under 'none' nothing is ever evicted for size, only expired entries are removed, so give every lock an expire. clear() releases every lock in the cache, so keep other data out of it: Cache('/var/cache/my-app/locks', eviction_policy='none').
Not on a NullCache or a durable=True cache. The recipes refuse them with TypeError: with caching off every caller would hold the lock at once, and a durable cache could drop the delete that releases one, leaving it held forever.
Not while waiting inside your own transaction. A recipe that would have to wait inside a transact() block on its own cache raises RuntimeError: waiting there holds the cache’s write lock, so no other process could ever release the lock you’re waiting for. Inside a transaction on a different cache, a contended recipe raises TransactionBusy at once rather than waiting (D-030).
On a FanoutCache each recipe locks only its key’s shard.
tag= tags every entry a recipe writes, so evict(tag) releases them all at once. barrier passes it to the lock factory only when it isn’t None.

title: Performance
text:
A microsecond is nothing until you multiply it. Web apps call their cache on almost every request, often straight from the asyncio event loop, where every microsecond the cache spends is a microsecond every other request on that loop waits. So diskcache-oxide’s performance work starts with read latency, then throughput under many threads, then predictable resource use. Correctness always comes first: every speedup has to keep the conformance suite green, or it doesn’t ship. The numbers below are the ones that survived.

The numbers
Measured with bench/gate.py, which runs python-diskcache 5.6.3 (its last release, from August 2023; the project has had no commits since) and diskcache-oxide in the same session on the same machine, in four interleaved rounds. These numbers come from Linux (Ubuntu 26.04 LTS) in a container on an Apple Silicon Mac. Both libraries ran in the same container, so the ratios compare like with like, but the absolute numbers on an x86-64 server will differ. Latencies are p50 in microseconds. Ratios are oxide’s time divided by diskcache’s, so lower is better.

Two things stand out:

On GIL builds, diskcache collapses as threads are added and oxide doesn’t. At 99:1, diskcache drops from about 375k to 44k operations per second going from 1 to 8 threads; oxide stays flat around 720-750k. diskcache’s per-thread connections end up fighting over the GIL and SQLite’s locks.
On free-threaded builds, oxide is faster at every thread count, but it doesn’t scale yet. 8 threads reach about 1.4M operations per second at 1,000:1, only 1.6× one thread. That’s what the free-threaded work below is for.

Run them yourself with python -m bench.gate. Numbers vary by machine; the ratios are what the gate enforces.


Where the speed comes from

Rust from the call to the disk. A get goes from Python straight into compiled Rust: one prepared SQLite statement, decode, done. There’s no Python wrapper in between.
Statements prepared once. Each pooled connection caches its prepared statements, so a lookup never recompiles SQL.
The clock is read in Rust. Checking expiry doesn’t call back into Python’s time.time().
Fast codecs. msgpack and tagged JSON are encoded and decoded in Rust, building Python objects directly.
Reads never write. Least-recently-stored eviction means a get never updates anything, so any number of readers proceed in parallel.
A smarter write lock. Writers in one process queue on an in-process lock per database file, instead of every thread retrying against SQLite’s busy handler.
SQLite tuned for it. The bundled SQLite is built with its global memory statistics turned off, which removes a process-wide mutex from every allocation: 2-10% more threaded throughput.



Prefix scans at scale
diskcache’s iterkeys() gets slower faster than the cache grows: about 1.7 seconds at 100,000 keys, and over 25 seconds at 400,000. diskcache-oxide’s iterkeys(prefix=...) is an indexed range scan, paged in batches so no read transaction is held between them. 400,000 keys scan in about 10 ms.


Memory that stays flat
Memory is bounded by configuration, not by how many threads touch the cache: at most max_connections connections per database file (default 8), each with a 1 MiB page cache. A FanoutCache defaults to two per shard for the whole root, about 16 MiB at 8 shards. A separate memory-instrumented build runs bench/memory.py and the memory tests under heavy load to hold that bound. See Storage and WAL.


Known slow spots
Two oversubscribed cases measure slower than before the SQLite mutex spin and the connection-slot spin went in. Both are known, and neither is in the path of a web app running a few threads per process.

A plain Cache with far more threads than cores, all sharing one handle: 7% slower on an M-series Mac at 36 threads, and 5% in a Linux VM at 32. Faster hand-off lets more threads into SQLite at once.
A FanoutCache at max_connections=32 with 8 threads, on macOS only: 5-12% slower. The same case on Linux is 41-56% faster.



Next: free-threaded scaling
Profiling a cached get shows that about 60% of its time is one system call: SQLite taking its shared-memory read lock on the -shm file, under a process-wide mutex. It’s the biggest single cost on every read, and it’s also what keeps free-threaded throughput from scaling. The free-threaded phase on the roadmap, after the Django backend, goes after it, along with:

a per-process lock-caching layer under SQLite, or longer-lived read snapshots;
thread-affine connections;
cheaper reference counting on shared Cache objects in free-threaded builds;
making threads that share one handle scale. FanoutCache is built and removes the multi-process write-lock ceiling, but at its default settings it doesn’t lift this read ceiling, so the shared per-handle path is being worked on.

Past that, the network server can go further still: as the only owner of its files, it can use SQLite’s exclusive locking mode, which keeps that lock in ordinary memory. Measured reads drop from 1.18 µs to 0.69 µs.

title: Switching from python-diskcache
text:
If you’re here, the question is a practical one: what breaks? Very little, and on purpose. diskcache-oxide is API compatible with python-diskcache 5.6.3’s Cache and FanoutCache, and it is not data compatible. Keeping diskcache’s API makes switching a one-line change. Leaving its on-disk format behind is what made it possible to fix the design underneath, pickle included. So the switch itself is small, and the rest of this page is about what you’ll notice afterwards: mostly fixes, and now and then something stricter.
diskcache is also unmaintained. Its last release, 5.6.3, came out in August 2023, the repository has had no commits since 2023, and its open issues and pull requests go unanswered. The bugs this page mentions were found by running diskcache-oxide’s test suite against it, and each one has a standalone reproduction in the repository’s upstream/ folder.
For most apps, switching looks like this:

title: Switching from python-diskcache
text:
Upgrading diskcache-oxide
During 0.x, a release that changes the on-disk format bumps the minor version and says so first in its changelog entry. 0.2.3 is one of them: it adds tags and the eviction policy to the format, so caches made by 0.1.2 have to be deleted when you upgrade. Stop every worker, delete the cache’s directory (a FanoutCache’s whole root, never one shard), and it’s recreated empty on the next open. Until you do, opening an old cache raises FormatMismatchError, which a Caches registry reports and answers with a NullCache. 0.1.2 refuses a 0.2.3 cache the same way, so old and new workers can’t share a cache during a rolling deploy. A release that keeps the format needs nothing.

title: Errors and what to do about them
text:
Sooner or later a traceback ends in diskcache_oxide, and the question is whether it’s your bug, an outage, or two processes disagreeing about what a directory is for. diskcache-oxide raises when something is wrong rather than guessing, and each exception is chosen so that except clauses you already have keep working: Timeout is a TimeoutError, TransactionAborted is a RuntimeError, UnsafeValueError is a TypeError, LayoutMismatchError is a ValueError. This page is the field guide: every exception, what it means, and what to do. The last section covers the log lines the library writes when it has been told not to raise, because then a log line is the only evidence you’ll get.








Exception

Where

any call that waits for a lock or a fork
