TypeError, ValueError, KeyError, RuntimeError, OSError, OverflowError, AssertionError, MemoryError
built-in
described below




TypeError at set(): a value that can’t be stored
TypeError: values of type Episode can't be stored without pickle (only exact built-in types round-trip)
The value isn’t one the msgpack or JSON format can represent exactly, so it’s refused where it was created rather than three requests later when something reads it. Only exact built-in types round-trip: str, bytes, int, float, bool, None, Decimal, and list, tuple, dict, set, frozenset, datetime and date made of those. A dataclass, an ORM row, a dict subclass or a class of your own doesn’t.
Fix it in this order:

Register the type: diskcache_oxide.register_type(Episode, name='tp.Episode') for a dataclass, or with encode= and decode= functions for anything else (an ObjectId, a namedtuple, a str subclass). The value is stored without pickle and comes back as the type you stored. See Your own types.
Or store a plain structure instead: a dict from a model’s model_dump(), and rebuild the object on the way out.
If you really need arbitrary objects, open a separate cache for them with Cache('/var/cache/my-app-objects', pickle=True). Don’t turn pickle=True on for a cache that other code shares just to make the error go away: every reader of that directory then runs pickle.loads on whatever is written there. See Serialization.

A registered type that still raises here is one whose encode function raised, or returned something the codec can’t store, or a dataclass with a field it can’t store. That raises even on a cache with pickle=True: a registered type is never pickled.


TypeError for keys and booleans
TypeError: cache keys must be str, bytes, int, float, bool, None, or a tuple of those, not list
TypeError: expire must be a number of seconds or None, not bool
Keys are str, bytes, int (64-bit), float, bool, None, or tuples of those. Only the exact types: a subclass such as an IntEnum or a namedtuple, a list or an int past 64 bits raises TypeError, and a NaN key raises ValueError, since it isn’t equal to itself. Pass a tuple where you’d use a list. A memoized function’s arguments follow the same rules, and the error names the argument. A bool where a number of seconds belongs (expire=True, timeout=True) is almost always an argument in the wrong position, so it’s refused rather than treated as 1, which is what diskcache does.


Timeout: a lock or a fork outlasted timeout
diskcache_oxide.Timeout: timed out after 1 s waiting for a lock or a pending fork
The call waited the cache’s timeout (60 s by default, or the timeout= passed to that call) and gave up. Something held what it needed, and there are three suspects:

Another writer held the write lock that long. One process at a time commits to a database file, and a burst of writes, a clear() from a maintenance script, or a long transact() block holds it. Reads never wait for writers, so a Timeout on a get is one of the next two cases.
A fork was pending. Before a fork, every cache call in the process waits for in-flight writes and then for the fork itself, and that counts against timeout. A fork takes about a millisecond in a quiet process and tens to hundreds of milliseconds beside busy threads on a GIL build. A timeout below that sees Timeout during ordinary forks. See How long a call waits for a fork.
Reading a large value kept losing to overwrites of the same key until timeout. Rare, and only on a key that’s rewritten flat out.

What to do:

In a request path, catch it and skip the cache. Give the cache a short timeout (Cache(path, timeout=1.0)), and treat Timeout as “don’t cache this time”: the value is a copy, and the request can go to the source of truth. Sharing a cache across web workers has the pattern.
Give maintenance its own timeout. clear(), expire() and cull() take timeout= for that call, and bound each chunk’s wait, so an admin page can pass clear(timeout=10) on a cache whose requests use 1 second. Run them from one scheduled job rather than from every worker.
Keep transact() blocks short, and never await inside one.
If many processes write often, use a FanoutCache. A plain Cache has one write lock per directory, and eight workers that all write queue on it. Sharding gives each shard its own.
Let the library answer it as a miss with durable=True: single-key calls then return their miss value instead of raising, and the failure is counted and logged. Pair it with a small timeout, since it doesn’t bound time on its own.
checkpoint() never raises Timeout: it returns False when other processes keep it busy. Call it again later, or at shutdown.



TransactionBusy: two caches in one transaction
Inside one cache’s transact() block, beginning a transaction on a second cache whose write lock another thread holds raises TransactionBusy at once instead of waiting. That thread could be waiting for the lock you hold, and then neither would ever finish. It’s a Timeout subclass, so existing handlers catch it, and retry=True never retries it.
Nest the two caches in the same order everywhere in your app. When TransactionBusy reaches you, leave the outer block, so your lock is released, and try the whole thing again. See Transactions.


TransactionAborted: a block that didn’t commit
TransactionAborted: the write transaction was rolled back after an error; nothing in it can commit
A with cache.transact(): block never exits cleanly when its writes are gone. This one comes from a write inside the block, or from the block’s exit, after one of its operations failed in a way that left the transaction unusable (a full disk, an I/O error).
TransactionAborted: the transaction did not commit: another thread or an earlier exit ended it, or it was rolled back after an error
This one comes from the block’s exit, when the transaction had already ended without committing: another thread rolled it back, or an earlier __exit__ call on the same object ended it (including one made from inside the block’s own operations, such as a pickle hook, which raises RuntimeError where it’s called and rolls the transaction back when that operation returns).
Either way nothing in the block was kept. Treat it as you would the original failure: log it, and run the block again if the work is idempotent. TransactionAborted is a RuntimeError, so an except RuntimeError you already have still catches it; catch TransactionAborted to handle this case alone.


RuntimeError from a transaction
RuntimeError: this database can't be written in a process forked inside a transaction
A process forked while the forking thread itself held a transact() block, and this is the child. The parent’s transaction carries on and commits; the child’s copy is poisoned, and its writes to that database raise this instead of stalling for a minute. Don’t fork from inside a transaction: start worker processes before the block, or after it. See Forking from inside your own transaction.


UnsafeValueError: a pickled value, read without pickle=True
UnsafeValueError: this value was stored with pickle; open the cache with pickle=True to read it
Two openers of one directory disagree about what it’s allowed to hold. A handle opened without pickle=True found a row that a pickle=True handle wrote, and refused to unpickle it, because unpickling runs whatever code the bytes describe. The row is left in place for the handle that can read it. This is a configuration mismatch, not damage, so it raises under every on_decode_error policy and under durable=True too.
Decide which the directory is for. If it holds pickled objects on purpose, open every handle on it with pickle=True. If it shouldn’t, find the writer that passed pickle=True and give it its own directory, then clear() this one. It’s a TypeError, like the error at set() above, because both come from the same decision: what this cache is allowed to hold.


CorruptValueError and ForeignValueError: a value that can’t be decoded
ForeignValueError: ...
CorruptValueError: ...
CorruptValueError means no build of diskcache-oxide could read the stored bytes: they’re malformed, a pickled class has been removed since it was stored, or a registered type’s decode function raised about the row (a dataclass row written before a field was removed, say), in which case your exception is its __cause__. ForeignValueError, its subclass, means this build can’t read them but another might: a newer version wrote a mode or tag this one doesn’t know, the value needs a time zone this host doesn’t have, or it holds a registered type this process hasn’t registered (the message names the tag: register it, at import time).
By default a read raises these, as diskcache does. A cache holds copies, so most apps would rather treat them as a miss:

Cache(..., on_decode_error='miss') returns the default, logs a warning on the diskcache_oxide logger, and deletes a row no build could read. A foreign row is kept, since the build that wrote it can still read it. durable=True turns this on by default.
Pass a function instead to report it yourself: on_decode_error=lambda key, exc: sentry.capture(exc). From a Caches registry it’s called as (name, key, exc).
For a ForeignValueError that keeps coming back, upgrade the older readers to the version that wrote the value, or stop the newer writer from sharing the directory. For a missing time zone, install the host’s zone data.

The full table of what each policy does with each failure is in Values that can’t be read.
CorruptKeyError, another subclass, comes from iterating a cache (for key in cache, iterkeys()) when a stored key’s bytes are damaged, which takes a damaged database page or file. Iteration raises rather than skip the key. Run cache.check() to see what else is damaged, or delete the directory: a cache can always start cold.


FormatMismatchError: a database this version can’t read
FormatMismatchError: cache format version 2 is not supported (this build uses version 3) (in /var/cache/my-app/diskcache-oxide.sqlite): it was made by an older diskcache-oxide: delete the cache's directory (a FanoutCache's whole root) with every process using it stopped, and it will be recreated empty
The directory holds a database, or a FanoutCache manifest, written in a format this build doesn’t know. Nothing is read or changed. The message says which way the versions differ:

Made by an older diskcache-oxide, as every cache made by 0.1.2 is after an upgrade to a release with format 3. Stop every process using the cache, delete the directory (for a FanoutCache, the whole root: one shard deleted alone would be recreated beside shards in the old format), and the next open creates it empty. A cache starts cold without harm. Don’t delete only the .sqlite file: its value files would be left behind.
Made by a newer diskcache-oxide: upgrade this process to match the writer, or point it at a different directory.



LayoutMismatchError: the wrong kind of cache for the directory
LayoutMismatchError: the root has 8 shards, not 16
The directory’s layout doesn’t match how it was opened: a plain Cache on a FanoutCache root or one of its shard directories, a FanoutCache on a plain Cache’s directory, or a shards= count that differs from the one the root records. The refused open creates nothing, so a typo doesn’t leave a directory neither kind can open. It’s both a ValueError and a FormatMismatchError.
Use the class the directory was created with, and for a FanoutCache either leave shards out (the stored count is used) or pass the stored one. A different shard count means a new directory: the count decides where every key lives, so it can’t change in place. See The layout and the hash. In a Caches registry, a lookup that hits a role mismatch returns a NullCache and reports it like any failed open. Another shard count is not an error there: the registry opens the folder with the count on disk and logs a warning (below). It still fails with LayoutMismatchError, and so a NullCache, when a size_limit or max_connections that fits the registered count is too small to split over the folder’s count; delete the folder or raise the setting.


RuntimeError: the filesystem can’t run SQLite in WAL mode
RuntimeError: the cache requires WAL journal mode, but SQLite is using "delete"
SQLite refused write-ahead logging, which diskcache-oxide requires for readers and a writer to work at the same time. That happens on network filesystems (NFS, SMB) and some FUSE mounts. The cache has to live on a local disk: /var/cache/<app>, or a Docker volume on the host’s disk. See Pick a directory.


OSError

Too many open files (errno EMFILE) opening a FanoutCache. Each shard takes about 4 file descriptors to open, so 256 shards need more than Linux’s usual ulimit -n of 1,024. The message gives the shard count, the descriptors needed, the limit and how many are already open. Raise the limit, or use fewer shards; eight is plenty for most apps. A failed open leaves nothing behind.
No hard links. Creating a FanoutCache manifest uses a hard link, so a filesystem without them (FAT, exFAT, SMB, some FUSE mounts) raises OSError saying so. Use a local disk.
Disk full, or an I/O error. The write didn’t happen and the cache is unchanged. Under durable=True a single-key call answers it as a miss or False and logs it; otherwise it raises. Timeout is an OSError too, so an except OSError around a cache call catches both.



ValueError

size_limit below 1 MiB. In diskcache a tiny limit silently evicts every value, including the one just stored; here it’s refused. For a FanoutCache the total must be at least shards MiB, since each shard needs 1 MiB.
max_connections below shards on a FanoutCache. Each shard needs at least one connection.
A key on another shard inside transact(key=...). The block covers one shard, and a call for a key elsewhere, reads included, can’t be atomic with it. Check with shard_of() that the keys share a shard, or keep them in one value.
A Caches name that’s taken, isn’t a plain directory name, or would share a directory with another registered cache.



KeyError

cache[key] and del cache[key] for a missing or expired key, as with a dict. Use get() and delete() for the “might not be there” cases.
incr(key, default=None) and decr(key, default=None) on a missing key. With the default default=0, a missing key starts counting from 0 instead.
Every NullCache[key], since nothing is ever present.



From the coordination recipes and the queue calls

TypeError: Lock needs a real cache: Lock, RLock, BoundedSemaphore, throttle, barrier and Averager refuse a NullCache and a durable=True cache, since with caching off every caller would hold the lock at once, and a durable cache could drop the write that releases it. Give them a cache of their own, opened without durable (see Coordination).
RuntimeError: Lock.acquire() would wait inside this thread's transaction: a recipe that would have to wait while you hold a transact() block on its own cache. Waiting there holds the write lock, so no other process could ever release what you’re waiting for. Take the lock before the block.
AssertionError from release() on an RLock you don’t hold, or a BoundedSemaphore released more often than it was acquired. It’s raised explicitly, so python -O doesn’t strip it.
OverflowError from push() after 500 trillion pushes to one end of a queue: it refuses rather than overwrite a key. A bad side raises ValueError.
UnsafeValueError, ForeignValueError or CorruptValueError from pull(). An item this process can’t read stays at the front of the queue for one that can, and one that no build could read is removed; see Work queues.



MemoryError
It always raises, under durable=True too, including when SQLite runs out of memory. A Caches lookup raises it as well, rather than handing out a NullCache.


Log lines, when the library was told not to raise
These settings turn failures into log lines on the diskcache_oxide logger instead of exceptions. Make sure that logger reaches your logging setup, since the line is then the only signal.

on_decode_error='miss' logs a warning for each stored version it couldn’t read, once per cache handle, and deletes the row if no build could read it.
durable=True counts every swallowed failure in one of three groups and logs each group’s first failure at once, then at most once a minute per cache handle, with counts by operation since its last line (get: 1204, set: 37). Busy (a Timeout) logs at WARNING, failing (a full disk, an I/O error, a damaged database) at ERROR, and lost invalidations (any failed delete, whose entry can now be served stale) at ERROR. An outage that ends within the minute shows only its first failure until the next line, so each line says more may follow. close() logs what’s left.
Caches logs could not open cache 'pages' at /var/cache/my-app/pages; using a NullCache, retrying in 10 s at ERROR with the traceback when a cache can’t open, and the same at WARNING without one when the open merely timed out (that’s retried after at most 1 s). Pass on_open_error= to send it to Sentry instead.
Caches also logs cache 'rate_limits' at /var/cache/my-app/rate_limits has 8 shards but is registered with shards=16; using the 8 on disk. To apply shards=16, delete /var/cache/my-app/rate_limits while no process has it open at WARNING each time it opens a sharded cache whose folder has another count than the registration, and once per process a FanoutCache is registered with a shard count its folder does not have at ERROR, a constant message with the details in the record’s cache, directory, stored_shards and registered_shards attributes, so an error tracker groups every worker’s report into one issue. The cache works throughout; this one doesn’t go through on_open_error, since the open succeeded.



If it looks like a bug in diskcache-oxide
If you’ve read this far and the traceback still doesn’t fit, it may be one. Open an issue with diskcache_oxide.__version__, diskcache_oxide.sqlite_version(), the interpreter (python -VV says whether it’s free-threaded), the platform and filesystem, how many processes and threads share the directory, and the full traceback. Every deliberate difference from diskcache is listed in Divergences, so check there first if the surprise is a behavior rather than an error.

title: Concurrency and forks
text: A production Python web app is a crowd. Several worker processes, often several threads in each, a pre-forking server that creates and recycles those workers while they’re busy, and a cron job or an admin script opening the same cache on the side. More and more, it’s also free-threaded Python, where the threads really do run at the same time. diskcache-oxide is designed for all of that at once, and its test suite runs each of these cases on every change, because this is where cache bugs hide: not in get and set, but in what happens when two of them collide.

title: Concurrency and forks
text:
A bounded connection pool
diskcache opens a SQLite connection for every thread that touches the cache and keeps it. With 64 threads that’s 131 open files in the cache directory, and a server with enough threads runs out of file descriptors.
diskcache-oxide shares a pool of connections per database file across every handle in the process:
cache = Cache('/var/cache/my-app', max_connections=8)   # the default
The pool never holds more than max_connections connections, so at most 2 × max_connections + 1 files are open in the cache directory, however many threads you run. A thread that finds every connection busy waits for one, up to the cache’s timeout. When the last handle on a directory closes, every connection closes with it, whichever threads used them.

title: Concurrency and forks
section: How long a call waits for a fork
text:
How long a call waits for a fork
A fork counts against timeout. A cache call behind a pending fork waits for it through the call’s own timeout and then raises Timeout, so timeout has to exceed the work in flight, plus the fork, plus the interpreter hand-off. A fork takes about a millisecond in a quiet small process, but tens to hundreds of milliseconds beside busy threads on a GIL build (the forking thread has to get the interpreter back), longer in a large process, and it waits for work in flight such as a forced checkpoint. A timeout under that sees Timeout during ordinary forks, and a loop on timeout=0 adds to the problem by being one of those busy threads.
A fork waits for every transaction another thread holds, with no timeout of its own, so a long transaction delays every fork in the process. Code that holds a transaction or runs inside a pickle hook (or a registered type’s decode function, which runs in the same place), and waits for another thread’s cache call, can keep a fork from finishing: the fork waits for that code, and the other thread waits for the fork. That other thread’s call now raises Timeout, and the fork finishes once your code lets go. Until it does, os.fork() doesn’t return, a second os.fork() queues behind it, and every thread with no transaction or hook of its own gets Timeout on every Cache in the process, after using up its whole timeout (60 seconds by default). Other processes aren’t affected. If the code never reacts (a hook that retries forever, or one blocked on something that isn’t a cache call), the fork stays stuck. A hook stuck in C code that holds the GIL stops everything, as it would without a cache.
Two calls don’t raise. checkpoint() returns False when a fork keeps it from running. close() takes at most about 2 seconds behind a stuck fork, 1 for the checkpoint and 1 for the release, and del about 1, whatever timeout is. An ordinary fork ends well inside that, so close() waits it out as usual. If the fork outlasts it, close() returns anyway and the connections close when the fork ends.
Before-fork hooks run in reverse registration order, and logging and concurrent.futures each take a lock in theirs and keep it until the fork is over. diskcache_oxide makes sure its own hook runs before those two, so they stay usable while a fork waits for your code: a pickle hook or a decode function can still log or submit work. Two things it can’t fix. Another library’s hook that takes a lock and is registered after diskcache_oxide stays held while a fork is stuck. And a thread that calls the cache while holding logging’s module lock can hold up a fork until that call’s timeout.
With durable=True, a Timeout behind a fork is a miss or False rather than an exception on a single-key call, so a timeout shorter than this makes ordinary forks into misses. A pickle hook or a registered type’s decode that re-raises the Timeout it got from another thread’s call lets go of its level under any policy, which clears the stuck fork. What durable=True adds is that the request doesn’t fail: that Timeout is a miss, with the row kept.

title: Concurrency and forks
section: Forking from inside your own transaction
text:
Forking from inside your own transaction
CPython won’t let a library refuse a fork, so the barrier can’t wait for a transaction held by the very thread that is forking. The child’s copy of that transaction is poisoned: anything done inside it raises RuntimeError and nothing commits, and the child’s writes to that database raise RuntimeError straight away instead of stalling for a minute. A transact() in the child doesn’t join the inherited transaction either: it raises RuntimeError too. The parent’s block carries on and commits as usual, and the parent gets a RuntimeWarning. A clear error at the call site beats a mysterious 60-second hang in a fresh worker.

title: New to caching? Start here
text:
If you’ve never put a cache in front of anything, this page is the ten minutes that make the rest of the docs read easily. If you have, skip to Getting started; nothing here is specific to diskcache-oxide except the examples.

What a cache is
A cache is a copy of an answer, kept somewhere cheaper to reach than wherever the answer came from. The database can tell you the ten most popular episodes, but it takes a few milliseconds and some of its attention to do it, and the answer is the same for everyone who asks in the next five minutes. So you ask once, keep the answer, and hand out the copy.
Something is worth caching when all three of these are true:

It’s asked for repeatedly. An answer nobody asks for twice is a copy nobody reads.
It costs something to produce. A database query, a call to another service, rendering a page, a calculation. A cache lookup costs about a microsecond in diskcache-oxide, so anything slower than that is a candidate, and anything that takes milliseconds is a good one.
A slightly old answer is acceptable, or you can tell when it stops being right. This is the one that bites, and the rest of this page is mostly about it.

Here it is in the smallest possible form. The first call does the work; the second gets the copy:

import tempfile
import time

from diskcache_oxide import Cache

cache = Cache(tempfile.mkdtemp())

def popular_episodes() -> list[str]:
    episodes = cache.get('episodes:popular')          # a hit returns the copy
    if episodes is None:                               # a miss: nothing cached, or it expired
        time.sleep(0.05)                               # stands in for the database query
        episodes = ['Rust for Python developers', 'Free-threaded Python', 'SQLite everywhere']
        cache.set('episodes:popular', episodes, expire=300)
    return episodes

for attempt in ('first call', 'second call'):
    start = time.perf_counter()
    popular_episodes()
    print(f'{attempt}: {(time.perf_counter() - start) * 1000:.2f} ms')

first call: 55.46 ms
second call: 0.02 ms


That shape, check the cache, do the work on a miss, store the result, is called cache-aside, and it’s the one you’ll use most. @cache.memoize() wraps it up as a decorator; the caching recipe shows how.


Why bother
Three reasons, and you usually get all three at once:

Latency. The page that took 300 ms takes 3, because the slow parts were answers you already had.
Load. The database answers a question once a minute instead of once a request. That’s the difference between a database that’s fine and one you’re upgrading at 2 a.m.
Protection. When the thing behind the cache is slow, flaky or rate-limited (a partner API, a search service), the cache keeps serving the last good answer while it recovers.

The flip side: a cache is a copy, and copies go out of date. Every design decision in caching is a trade between how fresh the answer is and how cheap it is to serve.


The words



Word
What it means




Hit / miss
A lookup found a live entry, or didn’t. The hit rate is the fraction of lookups that hit; a cache with a low hit rate is costing you writes for nothing.


Key
The name an entry is stored under. In diskcache-oxide a key is usually a string like user:42:profile; numbers, bytes and tuples such as ('user', 42) work too.


Expiry (TTL)
How long an entry stays valid. After it, a lookup misses as if the entry were gone. expire=300 means five minutes.


Stale
Still cached, but no longer what the source would say. Expiry bounds how stale an entry can get.


Invalidation
Removing or replacing an entry because its source changed, instead of waiting for it to expire.


Eviction
The cache removing entries to stay under its size limit. diskcache-oxide evicts the least recently stored entries first, or nothing at all under eviction_policy='none'. Eviction is why a cache can never be the only copy of something you need.


Cold / warm
A cold cache is empty (just deployed, just cleared) and every lookup misses until it’s warm. The first minutes after a deploy are the slow ones.


Stampede (thundering herd)
A popular entry expires and every worker recomputes it at the same instant. See Serving stale values while refreshing.


Negative caching
Caching “there’s no such thing” so a missing record doesn’t cost a database query every time someone asks. Use a short expiry.





The first hard thing: invalidation

There are only two hard things in Computer Science: cache invalidation and naming things.
Phil Karlton

(The popular extension adds “and off-by-one errors”, which is funnier if you don’t count.)
Invalidation is hard because the cache can’t know when the source changed. It has a copy of the answer; it has no idea the user just renamed themselves. Something has to tell it, and the three ways to do that are the whole of the art:

Let it expire. Give every entry an expire, chosen by how stale you can stand: five minutes for a popular list, an hour for a rendered page, a day for a thumbnail. It’s the simplest strategy, it needs no knowledge of where the data changes, and it’s the one safety net that catches every mistake in the other two. Always set an expiry, even when you also invalidate explicitly. An invalidation you forgot is otherwise forever.
Invalidate at the write. When your code saves the user’s new name, it also deletes user:42:profile. The next read misses and rebuilds. This gives exact freshness, at the cost of knowing every key the change affects, which is where naming (below) comes in. When many keys depend on one thing, delete them by prefix, store them with a shared tag and drop them all with evict(tag), or change a generation number so the old keys are never read again: Invalidating groups of keys.
Put the version in the key. If the key is episode:512:v7:page, then publishing revision 8 means readers ask for episode:512:v8:page, miss, and rebuild, and the old entry is simply never asked for again. Nothing is deleted; the stale copy expires on its own.

Most apps use all three: an expiry on everything, a delete where the write is obvious, and versioned keys for things that have a natural version. Here’s the expiry half, with a fake clock so it runs instantly:

now = [1_000_000.0]
cache = Cache(tempfile.mkdtemp(), clock=lambda: now[0])

cache.set('user:42:profile', {'name': 'Sam'}, expire=600)
print('right away:   ', cache.get('user:42:profile'))

now[0] += 601                                          # ten minutes pass
print('after expiry: ', cache.get('user:42:profile'))

cache.set('user:42:profile', {'name': 'Sam'}, expire=600)
cache.delete('user:42:profile')                        # the user renamed themselves: invalidate at the write
print('after delete: ', cache.get('user:42:profile'))

right away:    {'name': 'Sam'}
after expiry:  None
after delete:  None


One more rule that saves real grief: never cache a value that depends on who’s asking under a key that doesn’t say who’s asking. A profile page cached as page:profile will be shown to the next user who asks for it. If the answer depends on the user, the locale, the plan, or the A/B group, the key includes them.


The second hard thing: naming
Keys are names, and the two problems turn out to be the same problem: an invalidation can only find the entries whose names tell it what they depend on. Some conventions that hold up:

General to specific, separated by colons: user:42:profile, episode:512:transcript. Everything about user 42 then shares the prefix user:42:, and a prefix scan (iterkeys(prefix='user:42:')) finds all of it in time proportional to how many there are, not the size of the cache.
End a prefix with the separator. user:4 also matches user:42; user:4: doesn’t.
Include everything the value depends on, and nothing it doesn’t. A key with the request’s timestamp in it never hits. A key without the locale serves French pages to English readers.
Keys are cheap. A long, descriptive key costs almost nothing; a short, clever one costs you a debugging session later.



What goes wrong, and the fix

Stale data. Shorter expiry, or an invalidation at the write. If you can’t say which writes affect an entry, the expiry is your answer.
A stampede after a deploy or an expiry. Refresh hot entries ahead of time, or serve the stale copy while one worker rebuilds: Serving stale values while refreshing.
Cached errors. Don’t cache the result of a failed call as if it were an answer. Cache “not found” briefly if you must; never cache a 500.
Treating the cache as storage. An entry can be evicted or expire at any moment, and a deploy can clear the whole directory. Anything you can’t rebuild from somewhere else (a session, a one-time token, a counter you haven’t flushed) belongs in a cache of its own, opened with eviction_policy='none' so nothing is evicted for size, and ideally also somewhere permanent. The sessions and counters recipes show the pattern.
A bug that might be the cache. Turn caching off without touching the code that uses it, with NullCache, and see whether the bug survives.



Where diskcache-oxide fits
There are three usual places to keep a cache, and the choice is about who can see it and what survives:










A dict in the process
diskcache-oxide
A cache server (Redis)




Shared across worker processes
No, one copy per worker
Yes, every process on the machine
Yes, every machine


Survives a restart
No
Yes, it’s a directory
Depends on configuration


Cost of a lookup
Nanoseconds
About a microsecond
A network round trip


Something extra to run
No
No
Yes, a server



The in-process dict is unbeatable for a single process and useless the moment you have four gunicorn workers. The server is the right answer when the cache has to be shared across machines. diskcache-oxide is the middle: a cache that’s just a directory, shared by every thread and process on the machine, still there after a restart, and fast enough that you stop thinking about the lookup. Because every process sees the same directory, it also covers a few jobs people often run Redis for on a single machine: locks and rate limits, counters and work queues. Getting started is the next page.

title: Storage and WAL
text: Nobody restarts a cache. It sits inside a worker process for weeks, and whatever it does to memory and disk, it does slowly and out of sight, until an alert fires at a bad hour. So how much a cache uses has to be something you set, not something you discover. This page covers what diskcache-oxide puts on disk, and the settings that keep memory and disk where you put them.

title: Storage and WAL
text:
eviction_policy='none'
Some entries mustn’t disappear just because the cache got full: a lock, a job claim, the items in a work queue. For a cache that holds those, turn eviction off:
locks = Cache('/var/cache/my-app-locks', eviction_policy='none')
Under 'none', no write and no cull() evicts for size. Expired entries are still removed: each write sweeps up to cull_limit of them, expire() and cull() remove the rest, and cull() returns how many it removed. The cache can grow past size_limit, so give the entries an expire and keep them apart from your general-purpose cache, which should go on evicting.
The policy and both limits are stored in the cache, so every process shares them. Each write reads the policy afresh, so a change made from one process applies to every other at its next write, and a handle opened with eviction_policy=None (the default) keeps whatever is stored. reset() reads or changes one of them without reopening:
cache.reset('eviction_policy')            # 'least-recently-stored'
cache.reset('size_limit', 2 * 2**30)      # stored, and returned

title: Storage and WAL
text:
Always on: wal_size_limit
cache = Cache('/var/cache/my-app', wal_size_limit=64 * 1024 * 1024)   # the default
This tells SQLite to trim the log back to half the limit (32 MiB by default) whenever it resets, and scales how often SQLite checkpoints automatically. These are connection settings, so they never pause anything. At normal load they keep the log at a few MiB.

title: Storage and WAL
text:
On demand: checkpoint()
cache.checkpoint()   # True if the log was reset and truncated
checkpoint() copies the log into the database and truncates it to zero. It waits briefly for in-flight reads, retrying up to the cache’s timeout, and returns False instead of raising if other processes keep the database busy. Call it when a short pause suits your app: at shutdown, in a maintenance job, or after a large clear().

title: Storage and WAL
text:
At close
close() runs the same checkpoint when this is the process’s last handle on the cache and the log is over half the limit, waiting at most a second. A small log, the usual case, costs nothing extra. Pass close(checkpoint=False) to skip it.

title: Storage and WAL
text:
Opt-in: automatic checkpoints
cache = Cache('/var/cache/my-app', wal_checkpoint='auto')
With 'auto', writes check the log (at most every 250 ms or 64 writes) and checkpoint it when it’s over the limit, with the interpreter released. Readers in other processes can get in the way for a moment, so it tries the final truncation up to 8 times, a couple of milliseconds each, before backing off for a second. It never fails a write. It isn’t the default because on a saturated disk the write that triggers the checkpoint can still pause for a long time, and no write should pay for housekeeping unless you asked for it. The plan is to move this into a background maintenance thread so writes never pay for it at all. Writes queue behind a checkpoint for tens of milliseconds, so a timeout under about 35 ms can time out behind one.

title: Storage and WAL
section: The limit is a target, not a bound
text:
The limit is a target, not a bound
wal_size_limit says where the log should stay, not where it’s guaranteed to stay. Sustained writes from several processes near flat out can take it to tens of times the limit: we measured 6 GiB on free-threaded 3.15 and 21 GiB on 3.14 in 10 minutes, against a 64 MiB limit. It’s much smaller below flat out, for example 250 MiB at about 2,600 writes per second across 3 writers in auto.
In the default manual mode, with busy readers in other processes, the log grows until something checkpoints. If your app has that shape, use wal_checkpoint='auto' or call checkpoint() periodically. A script should call checkpoint() or close() after a large fill.

title: Serialization
text:
A cache has a quiet second job: it’s a program that reads bytes it didn’t write, left on disk by whatever process got there first. That makes the serializer the most security-relevant piece of the whole library, and it has three jobs. What goes into the cache should come out as exactly what you put in. Encoding and decoding should be fast, because they happen on every call. And reading the cache should never run code that someone else left there. diskcache’s default, pickle, does the first two well and fails the third by design: unpickling runs whatever the bytes tell it to. diskcache-oxide gets all three, and pickle becomes something you opt into, one cache at a time.

Two formats
Each cache picks a structured format with serializer=:
cache = Cache('/var/cache/my-app')                       # msgpack, the default
readable = Cache('/var/cache/my-app-json', serializer='json')

msgpack (the default) is compact and fast. On a 450 KB page-cache entry it’s about 25× faster than tagged JSON, and it stores nested bytes without base64.
json is human-readable: open diskcache-oxide.sqlite in any SQLite browser and read your values. It uses serde_json with exact float round-tripping. Keys aren’t JSON: str keys show as text, and keys of other types as a short binary encoding (see Keys and tags).

Plain str and bytes values skip both and are stored raw. Every row records how it was encoded, so if you change a cache’s serializer, existing entries stay readable.
Everything stored as a value goes through the same encoder: what you pass to set(), add() and push(), and what a memoized function returns.


Exact types
JSON turns tuples into lists and can’t store sets, datetimes, NaN, very large ints, or dicts with non-str keys. msgpack has some of the same gaps. The usual answer is to coerce quietly and let the bug show up later.
diskcache-oxide’s encoder, written in Rust, notices anything its format would change and tags it instead, so it decodes back to the same type:







Python value
Comes back as




tuple
a tuple, not a list


set
a set


frozenset
a frozenset


datetime.datetime
a datetime, with its timezone and microseconds


datetime.date
a date


decimal.Decimal
a Decimal, exact


int wider than 64 bits
the same int


float('nan'), inf, -inf
the same float


bytes nested in a container
bytes


dict with int (or other non-str) keys
the same keys



import datetime

cache.set('record', {
    'created': datetime.datetime.now(datetime.UTC),
    'point': (37.77, -122.42),
    'ids': {101, 102},
    'big': 2**128,
    'by_id': {1: 'one', 2: 'two'},
})

record = cache.get('record')
assert isinstance(record['point'], tuple)
assert record['by_id'][1] == 'one'
User data can’t be mistaken for a tag: a dict that happens to look like one is escaped on the way in and decoded as an ordinary dict on the way out.


What isn’t stored
A value that neither format can represent exactly, such as an instance of your own class, raises TypeError at set():
cache.set('service', MyService())
# TypeError: values of type MyService can't be stored without pickle (only exact built-in types round-trip)
Only exact built-in types count. A subclass of dict or str isn’t stored as its base type, because it wouldn’t come back as the class you stored. Failing at set() time means you find out where the value was created, not three requests later when something reads it. For a type of your own, or one from a library, register it.
A memoized function that returns such a value raises the same TypeError, after the function has run, when the result is stored. Nothing is cached, so the next call runs it again and raises again. Register the type, or have the function return something storable.


Your own types
Most of what an app stores that isn’t a built-in is a type it doesn’t own: a bson ObjectId inside a session dict, a namedtuple a library hands back, the str subclass a Markdown renderer returns. Converting those by hand at every call site works, but it’s the kind of code that drifts. Instead, tell the codec once how to store the type:
from bson import ObjectId
import diskcache_oxide

diskcache_oxide.register_type(ObjectId, name='bson.ObjectId', encode=str, decode=ObjectId)

cache.set('session', {'id': ObjectId(), 'user': ObjectId()})
cache.get('session')['id']   # an ObjectId again
encode turns an instance into a value the codec can already store, built-ins or other registered types, nested as deep as you like. decode turns that value back into an instance. The registration is process-wide, so make it at import time, in every process that opens the directory.
A dataclass needs only a name. Its init=True fields are read straight off the instance, with no intermediate dict, and on the way out it’s rebuilt with cls(**fields), so defaults and __post_init__ still run:
@dataclasses.dataclass
class Episode:
    id: int
    title: str
    published: datetime.datetime | None = None

diskcache_oxide.register_type(Episode, name='tp.Episode')
cache.set('episode:491', Episode(491, 'Rust and Python'))
The write path skips dataclasses.asdict(), which deep-copies: on a 20-field dataclass a set() goes from about 23 µs to 18. A read still builds one keyword dict and calls the constructor, so it saves almost nothing (4.0 µs against 3.8), and that’s fine: a cache is mostly reads, and what you gain is the call sites.
What the registry guarantees:

Nothing is imported by name. A registered value is stored as {"$t:bson.ObjectId": "..."}, and a reader looks that name up in its own registry. A process that hasn’t registered it gets ForeignValueError, and the row stays for one that has. That is the whole difference from pickle.
The name is yours. Rename or move the class and the stored rows still read, because the tag is the name you chose, not the class’s path.
Lookup is by exact type. A subclass of a registered class is its own registration. The codec’s own types (str, dict, datetime and the rest) can’t be registered, since their wire form is a contract across versions; their subclasses can, which is how a namedtuple or a str subclass gets in.
A registered type is never pickled, even on a cache with pickle=True. Once the encoder has used a registration for any part of a value, that value is stored through it or set() raises: if its encode raises, or returns something the codec can’t store. You registered it to stay off pickle, and a silent fallback would hide the bug.
Last registration wins, by class and by name, so a module that a dev server reloads can register its new class object again.
A decode function’s errors are classified as a pickle hook’s would be. A Timeout or OSError raises with the row kept (a miss under durable=True). An error about the row, such as a TypeError from a dataclass row written before a field was removed, becomes CorruptValueError with yours as __cause__, and on_decode_error='miss' deletes that row so the writer replaces it. Decode runs while the cache holds a connection, as unpickling does, so a slow decode delays forks and checkpoints for as long as it runs; one that re-enters the cache is fine.

A cache that needs a different encoding of a type than the rest of the process gets its own registry, consulted before the global one:
reg = diskcache_oxide.TypeRegistry()
reg.register(ObjectId, name='bson.ObjectId', encode=lambda o: o.binary, decode=ObjectId)
cache = Cache('/var/cache/my-app-binary-ids', types=reg)
Two processes with different registrations on one directory write rows the other can’t read, the same way two processes with different serializer= settings would. Register at import time, the same way everywhere.


Why pickle is off by default

Unpickling runs code. Anyone who can write to the cache directory, including a compromised neighbor process or a shared volume, can make every reader run arbitrary Python.
Pickle hides mistakes. Database sessions, open files and other objects that were never meant to be cached get pickled without complaint and fail later in confusing ways.



Opting in to pickle
When you really do need to cache arbitrary objects, turn pickle on for that cache. It’s used only for values the structured format can’t represent; everything else is still stored as msgpack or JSON.
objects = Cache('/var/cache/my-app-objects', pickle=True)
objects.set('service', MyService())
A good habit is to give pickled values their own cache directory, and keep everything else in a cache without pickle.


Reading safely: UnsafeValueError
Several processes can open one directory with different settings. A handle opened without pickle=True never unpickles. If it reads a value that a pickle=True handle stored, it raises diskcache_oxide.UnsafeValueError (a TypeError subclass) and leaves the row in place, so the pickle=True handle can still read it.
A value whose stored bytes can’t be decoded at all raises CorruptValueError (a ValueError subclass).


Keys and tags
Keys follow stricter rules than values, because a key has to be compared, sorted and found as well as read back. They never go through serializer=, pickle= or the type registry. A key can be:

str, bytes, bool or None
an int that fits in 64 bits
a float, except NaN, which raises ValueError because it isn’t equal to itself
a tuple of any of these, nested up to 32 deep

cache.set(('episode', 491, 'transcript'), text)
cache.set(b'\x9f\x02', blob)
cache.set(42, 'the answer')
Anything else raises TypeError, even on a pickle=True cache: a list, a dict, a bytearray, an object, a registered type, and subclasses such as an IntEnum, a StrEnum or a namedtuple. If your key is an enum member, use its .value; if it’s a namedtuple, pass tuple(point).
Keys compare by exact type, so 1, 1.0 and True are three different keys. Python’s == says they’re equal, and diskcache treats 1 and 1.0 as one key, so code that mixes them finds nothing where it expected a hit. The exception is -0.0, which is the same key as 0.0, as it is in a dict.
A str key is stored as plain text. Every other key is stored in a compact binary encoding that sorts the way the values do, which is why iterkeys() can walk them in order: every str key first, then None, the bools, ints, floats, bytes and tuples, each group sorted. iterkeys(prefix=...) matches str keys only, so if you plan to list or delete a group of keys by prefix, make them strings ('user:42:profile', not ('user', 42, 'profile')).
A memoized function’s key is a tuple built from its name and its arguments, so every argument it’s called with must be one of these types. A call with a list or an object raises TypeError before the function runs. Leave arguments like a database connection out of the key with ignore=.
Tags, from set(..., tag=...) and memoize(tag=...), follow the same rules as keys and are stored the same way. evict(1) removes entries tagged 1 and leaves the ones tagged 1.0 or True.

title: FanoutCache: sharded caches
text: A plain Cache has one write lock per database file, which makes it a shop with one checkout lane: readers walk straight through, but every writer queues, and eight worker processes that all bump counters are eight carts in one lane. A FanoutCache opens more lanes. It’s one cache spread over several SQLite databases, called shards. Each key lives in exactly one shard, chosen by a fixed hash of the key, so writes to different keys go to different files and stop queueing on one lock. It has the same methods as Cache for single keys, and it’s one directory, shared by any number of threads and processes.

title: FanoutCache: sharded caches
section: Plain Cache and FanoutCache directories don’t mix
text:
Plain Cache and FanoutCache directories don’t mix
A Cache opened on a FanoutCache’s directory, or on one of its shard directories, raises LayoutMismatchError, and so does a FanoutCache opened on a plain Cache’s directory. The refused open creates nothing, so a typo doesn’t leave a directory that neither kind can open. LayoutMismatchError is both a ValueError and a FormatMismatchError. If a registry hits it, the lookup returns a NullCache and reports it like any failed open. A registry that meets another shard count than its registration’s opens the folder with the count on disk and warns instead (Caches).

title: Transactions
text:
Every write is already its own transaction, atomic across every thread and process using the directory. Sometimes one write at a time isn’t enough. A request bumps a total, bumps a per-path counter and records when it happened, and a reader that sees two of those three has seen something that was never true. transact() groups several calls into one: they all commit together when the block exits, or none of them do.
That’s also faster. Each commit costs a disk sync, so grouping writes pays for one instead of several: three counter bumps measured 79 µs one by one and 48 µs in one transaction.

title: Transactions
text:
Two caches at once: TransactionBusy
Inside one cache’s transaction, beginning a transaction on a second cache takes that cache’s write lock if it’s free. If another thread holds it, transact() raises TransactionBusy at once instead of waiting: that thread could be waiting for the lock you hold, and then neither would ever finish. TransactionBusy is a subclass of Timeout, so existing handlers still catch it, and retry=True never retries it, since trying again while you still hold the first lock can’t help.
To use two caches in one block, always nest them in the same order everywhere in your app, and if TransactionBusy reaches you, leave the outer block and try the whole thing again.

title: Transactions
text:
Ending it from another thread
diskcache says a transaction “may not be shared between threads”. In diskcache-oxide, any thread may call the transaction’s __exit__, to commit (no exception) or roll back the owner’s transaction. The rules:

While the owner is inside one of its own operations (decoding a value, say), a rollback is left to that operation, and happens when it returns. A commit waits for it, up to the cache’s timeout. A commit that can’t run by then raises Timeout and rolls back.
The owner’s own exit afterwards raises TransactionAborted unless the transaction committed.
An owner’s exit that comes while the other thread is still committing waits for the outcome, up to the cache’s timeout, and reports it. Past that, it raises Timeout (“whether it committed is unknown”). An exit with an exception passing doesn’t wait.
Writes the owner makes after another thread ended the transaction run on their own, outside it.

title: Vision and roadmap
text:
A shared cache is one of the first pieces of infrastructure a Python web app grows into, and today the choice is awkward. An in-process dict is fast, but each worker has its own copy and it’s gone on restart. Redis is shared and durable, but it’s a separate server, a network hop on every read, and one more thing to run. python-diskcache showed there’s a lot of room between those two: a cache that is just a directory, shared by every thread and process on the machine, built on SQLite. diskcache itself has had no commits since 2023, and its issues and pull requests go unanswered, so the idea needed a new home.
diskcache-oxide is a bet that this middle option can be much bigger than it has been. With a Rust engine underneath, a directory-backed cache can be fast enough to call on the event loop, safe enough for pre-forking servers and free-threaded Python, and complete enough to cover the jobs people now reach for Redis to do: caching, counters, rate limits, locks, job claims and queues. And when one machine isn’t enough, the same engine can be served over the network.
It’s being built in three stages.


Keep diskcache’s API, fix what’s wrong underneath it, and make it fast. With 0.2.3, everything from diskcache’s Cache and FanoutCache that real apps use is in. Behavior comes first: every phase keeps a conformance suite green against real diskcache 5.6.3 before chasing speed, and every deliberate difference is written down in Divergences.



The things a modern Python stack needs that diskcache never had. Sharding that doesn’t lock every shard for a transaction and coordination recipes that hold across every process are already in. Still to come are a Django cache backend, threads that scale on free-threaded Python, and an async API.



The same Rust core, served over HTTP to many clients: a Redis-style central cache with SQLite underneath, for when your app outgrows one machine. A server that is the only owner of its files can run SQLite in exclusive locking mode, which keeps the WAL index in heap memory instead of a shared file. title: Vision and roadmap
text:
Done: concurrency review and soak
The concurrency core is where serious bugs hide, so it got its own phase before anyone ran it in production: independent deep reviews by several AI coding agents, model-checker tests for the lock state machines, and day-long soak runs with many processes and threads, forks, SIGKILLs and clear() under load, checking for corruption, lost writes, leaks and latency drift. The 24-hour soak passed, and it paid for itself along the way: it found the unbounded WAL growth that wal_size_limit and checkpoint() now rein in. The limit is a target, not a bound: several processes writing flat out can still take the log well past it (see Storage and WAL).

Next

What

A diskcache-oxide backend for Django’s cache framework, tested against Django’s own cache test suite. It’s a big job, so it gets a phase of its own.

Make throughput scale with threads on 3.14t and 3.15t. Today a cached read spends about 60% of its time in one system call SQLite makes for its shared-memory lock, and that’s the first target.

title: Vision and roadmap
text:
Decided against, and why

Least-recently-used and least-frequently-used eviction. diskcache implements them by writing to the database on every get. Reads that never write are what let many processes read at once without queueing, so these stay out unless a design keeps reads write-free. Least-recently-stored stays the default, and eviction_policy='none' turns eviction off.
Deque and Index, until someone asks. If you need one, open an issue. An Index is only as general as the key types, and both default to a temporary directory, which diskcache-oxide doesn’t do.
disk= and Disk subclasses. A Python class on every read and write would undo the Rust engine; serializer= and register_type() cover what people used them for.
Pickled keys. Keys are never pickled, so listing keys never runs pickle and a key’s identity doesn’t depend on pickle’s bytes.
read=True and read() (streaming a file in and out). Folded into the large-file cache idea below.
Persisted statistics. stats() counts per process, in memory, because diskcache’s persisted counters make every get a write.

title: Getting started
text: A Cache is a directory. That’s the whole mental model, and it carries further than it looks: open the same directory from any number of threads and processes and they all share one cache, nobody has to be told about anybody else, and the entries are still there after a restart, because a directory doesn’t restart. Hold on to that sentence; most of what follows is a consequence of it. This page covers installing diskcache-oxide, the everyday operations, the handful of things that only start to matter once several processes are involved, and how to shut down cleanly.

title: Getting started
text:
Close it, or use with
with Cache('/var/cache/my-app') as cache:
    cache.set('greeting', 'hello')
close() returns the handle’s SQLite connections. Once the last handle on a directory in a process closes, nothing in that directory is held open, so it’s safe to move or delete.

title: Getting started
text:
Dictionary syntax
cache['alpha'] = 100
assert 'alpha' in cache
assert cache['alpha'] == 100
del cache['alpha']        # KeyError if it's missing, like a dict

title: Getting started
text:
Remove values
cache.delete('user:42')             # True if it was there
value = cache.pop('session:7')      # the value, or the default if it was missing

title: Getting started
Getting started
text:
What a dropped call costs
A failure reaches you as “wasn’t there”, so know what each one means before you turn this on.

A dropped set, delete, pop or version-bump incr serves stale data. The old entry stays. It’s served until it expires, and with no expiry that means forever, or until a later write replaces it. delete returns False, the same as for a key that wasn’t there, so your code can’t tell. The log line is the only signal. If stale data would be a real problem, give those entries an expiry.
A pop whose delete fails returns the default, not the value, since the row is still there and a later pop could deliver the value a second time.
A fake incr isn’t a count. It’s what a NullCache returns, so a rate limiter fails open. Don’t use one as an id: two callers can get the same number.
add fails closed. It returns False under durable=True, but True on a NullCache, so Caches can give you either answer for one key. Use a separate handle without durable for claims and locks, and treat its exceptions as “not claimed”.

title: Getting started
text:
It doesn’t bound time
A call still waits up to its timeout before it gives up, so pair durable=True with a small timeout=. Not too small: timeout still has to exceed the work in flight, plus a fork, plus the interpreter handing over, or ordinary forks turn into misses. Beside busy threads on a GIL build, that hand-over alone takes tens to hundreds of milliseconds. See How long a call waits for a fork.

title: Getting started
text:
Reporting
Every swallowed failure is counted in one of three groups, and logged on the diskcache_oxide logger, so one group can’t hide another:








Group
Level
What’s in it




Busy
WARNING
Timeout: a lock or a fork outlasted timeout


Failing
ERROR
Everything else: a full disk, an I/O error, a damaged database


Lost invalidations
ERROR
Any failed delete



Each group logs its first failure at once, then at most once a minute per cache handle, with counts by operation since its last line: get: 1204, set: 37. An outage can be thousands of failures a second, and that’s one line a minute. Failures after a group’s last line stay counted until its next one, or until you call close(), which logs what’s left. Dropping a handle without close() doesn’t. An outage that ends within the minute can therefore show only its first failure until then, which is why each line says more may follow. A hook outage on a read is reported once per stored version, as in the pop table above, and counted here as busy for a timeout and failing otherwise, with no line of its own: the group’s next line includes it. Time comes from the failing call’s clock, so clock= drives it in tests. cache._durable_stats() has the running totals by group and operation, the place to look for “how many invalidations did we lose?”. It’s a private hook for now, like _wal_stats().
The limit is per handle, so a with Cache(...) per request logs on every request during an outage. A handle from Caches is opened once, so it isn’t affected.

title: NullCache
text:
Sooner or later you need to turn caching off. In tests, so each one starts clean. In local development, so you see your change instead of yesterday’s. In production, at the worst possible moment, while you chase a bug that might be a stale entry and might not. Without help, that means if cache is not None: around every call, or a hand-written fake that drifts a little further from the real API with every release.
NullCache is a cache that’s switched off. It has the same methods and signatures as Cache, so swapping one for the other is a one-line change, and the code that uses it never knows.

title: NullCache
text:
Watch add()
The rule means add() always succeeds on a NullCache. If you use add() to claim a job so only one worker runs it, then with caching off every worker’s claim succeeds and the job runs once per worker. That’s harmless for idempotent work and wrong for work with side effects, like sending email. Keep claims like that on a cache that’s never switched off.
Cache(durable=True) goes the other way: its add() returns False when a write fails, so a claim fails closed there and open here. Keep claims on a handle that isn’t durable and handle its exceptions. See A cache that can’t take a request down.
The coordination recipes won’t run on a NullCache at all. Lock, RLock, BoundedSemaphore, Averager, throttle and barrier raise TypeError, because a lock that every caller holds at once is worse than no lock. memoize_stampede is a cache rather than a lock, so it runs on one the way memoize does, calling the function every time.

title: NullCache
text:
Watch the queue calls
A queue on a NullCache is always empty. push() returns the key an empty queue’s first item would get and stores nothing, so with caching off every job you push is lost, and pull() on the other side never sees it. Keep a work queue on a cache that’s never switched off, as you would a claim.

title: Caches: named caches
text:
Every app with two caches eventually grows a file called something like cache_service.py. It maps names to directories, opens each cache once and hands out the same object afterwards, carries on with caching switched off when a directory can’t be opened, lets you turn one off for a load test, and feeds counts and sizes to an admin page. It’s the same file in every app, written slightly differently each time. Caches is that file, so you don’t have to write it again.
Settings passed to Caches apply to every cache, and register can override them for one. Each cache lives in a directory named after it under the base directory, unless you pass directory=.
One setting works differently here: a function passed as on_decode_error is called as report(name, key, exc), with the cache’s name first, so one reporter can serve every cache. (On a plain Cache it’s report(key, exc).) A function that doesn’t take three arguments is rejected when you create the registry or register the cache.

title: Caches: named caches
section: After an upgrade that changes the format
text:
After an upgrade that changes the format
0.2.3 changes the on-disk format, so every cache made by 0.1.2 fails to open with FormatMismatchError once a worker runs the new version. In a registry that’s an ordinary open failure. Each lookup gets a NullCache, the error is logged at ERROR (or passed to your on_open_error) each time the open is retried, and requests keep working without that cache. The message names the directory to delete.
It stays that way until the old directory is gone. Delete it, and the next retry, within retry_open_after seconds, creates the cache empty and hands out the real one again, with no restart. The clean way is to do it during the deploy: stop every worker, delete the cache directories (a sharded cache’s whole folder, never one shard inside it), then start the new version. Workers still running 0.1.2 can’t use a cache the new version created either, so don’t leave old and new workers running side by side on the same caches. Upgrading diskcache-oxide has the details.

title: diskcache-oxide
text:
diskcache-oxide
A shared, durable disk cache for Python, with a Rust engine, SQLite storage, and a diskcache-compatible API.
Python cache. Rust engine. SQLite storage.
Every Python web app arrives at the same crossroads. A query that was fine at launch is now the slowest thing on the page, so you cache its result in a dict, and for one afternoon you’re a hero. Then the app goes under gunicorn with four workers, and there are four dicts, each warming up alone and each forgetting everything the moment its worker is recycled. So you reach for Redis, and now there’s a server to deploy, secure, monitor and pay for, whose entire job is to remember the answer to one query.
python-diskcache showed there was a third road: a cache that is just a directory. Every thread and every process on the machine opens the same path and sees the same entries, and the entries are still there tomorrow, because a directory doesn’t restart. No daemon, no network hop, no second system to keep alive. It’s the kind of idea that sounds too simple to be fast, and for years that was the catch. diskcache itself has had no commits since 2023, and its issues and pull requests go unanswered.
diskcache-oxide removes the catch. It keeps the diskcache API you already know and rebuilds everything beneath it for where Python is going: many cores, many worker processes, free-threaded CPython, and async frameworks that can’t afford a slow call on the event loop. The engine is Rust. The storage is SQLite. The Python layer is as thin as it can be. One thread gets nearly 600,000 cache operations a second out of a Cache, and eight threads sharing it still get that rate while python-diskcache’s falls below 20,000. Nothing on your disk is a pickle unless you asked for one, and memory and disk use stay where you set them.
Source on GitHub: https://github.com/mikeckennedy/diskcache-oxide · Issues
Here is the whole idea on one screen. Four workers, one directory. The cache makes the slow query cheap, and add() elects exactly one worker to run the hourly job, because a write that’s atomic across processes is a lock if you squint:
And here is what it does under load. Every thread shares one cache, the x axis adds threads, and the two libraries go in opposite directions:

title: diskcache-oxide
text:
Where this is going
diskcache-oxide is being built in three stages. The first is done and the second is mostly done.

A better diskcache. The Cache and FanoutCache you already know, rebuilt in Rust: about half the read latency, many times the threaded throughput, safe across fork(), safe on free-threaded Python, and no pickle by default.
The complete local caching toolkit. Keys of every native type, memoize, tags, work queues, transact() and the coordination recipes (locks, semaphores, throttles, stampede protection) are all here. Still to come in this stage are a Django cache backend, free-threaded scaling, and a native AsyncCache for FastAPI, Litestar and friends.
A cache server. The same Rust engine served over the network: a Redis-style central cache for a fleet of machines, with SQLite underneath instead of RAM. As the only owner of its files, the server can use SQLite’s exclusive locking mode, which already measures about 40% faster reads than the shared-directory library.

See Vision and roadmap for how each stage breaks down.

title: diskcache-oxide
text:
Why diskcache-oxide

Fast where web apps spend their time. At a 99:1 read/write mix, one thread gets about 590,000 operations a second from a Cache, 1.6× diskcache’s rate and cheap enough to call straight from the event loop. Add threads and the gap opens: at 8 threads on a GIL build, diskcache’s per-thread connections pile into each other and its throughput falls to 15,000 a second, while oxide’s stays near 570,000, 38× ahead (the chart above).
Built for free-threaded Python. The extension is compiled with gil_used = false and never leans on the GIL for correctness, which matters on a build where there’s no GIL to lean on. Every change is tested on 3.14, 3.14t, 3.15 and 3.15t.
Safe across fork(). gunicorn, Celery’s prefork pool and multiprocessing create workers by copying the parent, and the copy includes whatever SQLite lock a thread was holding at that instant. A process-wide fork barrier makes sure no child is ever born holding half a transaction.
No pickle on your disk. Values are msgpack (or JSON) with exact type tags, so tuples, sets, datetimes, dates, Decimals, big ints and NaN come back as what you stored, not as whatever the format could manage. Your own types are registered once and read back only where the name is registered. Pickle is opt-in, and a cache that didn’t opt in refuses to unpickle anything it finds, however it got there.
Predictable memory and disk. A bounded connection pool, a 1 MiB page cache per connection, a write-ahead log that trims itself back down, and a checkpoint() for when you want it empty now.
Correct under pressure. clear() never deletes writes that landed while it ran, a reader racing an overwrite gets the old value or the new one, never a spurious miss, and a queue never hands a worker another queue’s items or loses one it couldn’t read. Running the same test suite against both libraries turned up 18 bugs in diskcache, each with a reproduction in the repo, and each fixed here.
More than get and set. memoize caches a function’s results by its arguments. Tags group entries so evict(tag) removes a user’s or a page’s in one call. push and pull make a work queue every worker shares, handing each item to exactly one of them. Locks, semaphores and rate limits hold across every process on the machine, with no Redis.
A real off switch. NullCache turns caching off without a single if cache is not None: in your code, and can keep forwarding invalidations to the real cache while it’s off, so nothing stale is waiting when you turn it back on.
Named caches with an off switch. Caches registers an app’s caches once, opens each on first use, hands out a NullCache while one can’t open, and gives an admin page its counts and sizes.
Errors you can act on. Every exception says what went wrong, in words, and the errors page says what to do about it. Nothing is swallowed unless you turned on the setting that swallows it.
Typed. Ships py.typed and a CacheLike protocol that Cache, FanoutCache and NullCache all satisfy.

diskcache-oxide runs in production at Talk Python, Python Bytes and Talk Python Training. Every release runs three gauntlets first. A conformance suite runs the same tests against diskcache 5.6.3 itself, and every place the two differ is a deliberate decision, written down with its reason in Divergences. A sanitizer pass puts the whole codebase, bundled SQLite included, under Miri, ThreadSanitizer (with a free-threaded CPython built under it too), AddressSanitizer and LeakSanitizer. And a 24-hour soak throws processes, threads, forks, SIGKILL and clear() under load at one directory for a day, then checks it for corruption, lost writes and leaks.
Most of diskcache’s API is here: Cache and FanoutCache, keys of every native type, memoize, tags and evict(), transact(), the queue calls push, pull and peek, retry=, stats(), check(), eviction_policy='none', and the coordination recipes. Still to come: Deque and Index, reading a large value as a file (read=), AsyncCache, a Django cache backend, and Windows. Custom disk= classes and least-recently-used eviction aren’t coming; Vision and roadmap says why.

title: diskcache-oxide
text:
Install

It supports CPython 3.14 and 3.15, including the free-threaded builds (3.14t and 3.15t), on macOS and Linux. Wheels cover macOS on Apple Silicon and Linux (glibc) on x86_64 and aarch64 for all four Pythons, with the compiled engine and a bundled SQLite inside, so there’s nothing else to install.
